57951.e: In the Mariana Trench, the old, heavy Pacific Plate pushes beneath the Philippine Plate. The island arc of the Marianas lies above the subduction zone.
57951.m: At the Mariana Trench, the Pacific Plate sinks beneath the Philippine Plate.

57952.q: Which oceanic plate sinks off the west coast of South America and creates the volcanoes of the Andes?
57952.e: The Nazca Plate pushes beneath the South American Plate. This created the Peru-Chile Trench and the volcano-rich Andes.
57952.m: The Nazca Plate sinks beneath South America and feeds the Andean volcanoes.

57953.q: Which small plate sinks beneath North America and feeds the volcanoes of the Cascade Range?
57953.e: The Juan de Fuca Plate is a remnant of the former Farallon Plate. Its sinking off Oregon, Washington and British Columbia creates volcanoes such as Mount Rainier.
57953.m: The Juan de Fuca Plate feeds the volcanoes of the Cascade Range.

57954.q: What do you see if you plot the earthquake foci at a subduction zone by their depth?
a: They get deeper with increasing distance from the trench
They all lie exactly at the Earth's surface
They all lie in the Earth's core
They are spread completely at random
57954.e: The earthquake foci follow the slanting, sinking plate down to a depth of around 700 km. This zone is called the Wadati-Benioff zone.
57954.m: The Wadati-Benioff zone traces the sinking plate with earthquake foci.

57955.q: Why are there practically no volcanoes along the San Andreas Fault in California?
a: The plates slide sideways past each other there
A plate sinks very steeply there
The magma freezes in thick ice
57955.e: The San Andreas Fault is a transform fault. Because no plate sinks and none drift apart there, hardly any magma forms, but there are strong earthquakes.
57955.m: A transform fault produces earthquakes but hardly any volcanoes.

57956.q: Which island nation in the south of the Pacific Ring of Fire suffered a devastating earthquake in the city of Christchurch in 2011?
57956.e: On 22 February 2011, a shallow earthquake of magnitude 6.2 hit Christchurch and killed 185 people. New Zealand lies on the boundary between the Pacific and Australian Plates.
57956.m: New Zealand lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire and is often hit by earthquakes.

57957.q: What is the chain of underwater mountains called that continues the Hawaiian chain to the north?
57957.e: The Hawaiian-Emperor chain is around 6,000 km long. Its northern part, the Emperor Seamounts, reaches as far as the Aleutian Trench.
57957.m: The Emperor Seamounts continue the Hawaiian chain to the north.

57958.q: Roughly how many years ago did the striking bend between the Hawaiian chain and the Emperor Seamounts form?
57958.e: The bend is dated to around 47 million years ago. It shows a change in the plate's movement or a movement of the hotspot itself.
57958.m: The bend in the Hawaiian-Emperor chain is about 47 million years old.

57959.q: How fast does the Pacific Plate move over the Hawaiian hotspot?
a: A few millimetres per thousand years
57959.e: The Pacific Plate moves north-west at around 7 to 10 cm per year. That is why the volcanoes are carried away from the hotspot over time.
57959.m: Each year the Pacific Plate moves a few centimetres over the hotspot.

57960.q: Which of these Hawaiian islands is geologically the oldest?
57960.e: The islands get older and older towards the north-west, because the plate carries them away from the hotspot. Kauaʻi is around 5 million years old, the island of Hawaiʻi less than 1 million years.
57960.m: The further north-west a Hawaiian island lies, the older it is.

57961.q: What will probably form in the distant future south-east of the island of Hawaiʻi over the hotspot?
a: An atoll with no volcano beneath it
57961.e: An underwater volcano, Kamaʻehuakanaloa (formerly Lōʻihi), is already growing over the hotspot south-east of Hawaiʻi. It is still around 1,000 m below sea level and could one day form a new island.
57961.m: The next Hawaiian island is already growing over the hotspot.

57962.q: What does the hotspot theory explain about the Hawaiian Islands?
a: Why the islands get older towards the north-west
Why Hawaii lies exactly on a plate boundary
Why there are no earthquakes on Hawaii
Why the islands are made of granite
57962.e: In 1963, J. Tuzo Wilson interpreted the age sequence of the islands as the track of a plate moving over a fixed source of melt. The volcanoes therefore get older with distance from the hotspot.
57962.m: The hotspot theory explains the age sequence of the Hawaiian Islands.

57963.q: According to a widely held hypothesis, from what depth do mantle plumes like the one beneath Hawaii come?
a: From the base of the lithosphere
57963.e: Many geophysicists think that hot rock rises from the boundary between the Earth's core and mantle. Seismic images show a hot zone reaching deep down beneath Hawaii.
57963.m: The Hawaiian plume probably rises from the core-mantle boundary.

57964.q: Why do the old atolls at the north-western end of the Hawaiian chain gradually sink into the sea?
a: The base sinks and the corals grow back too slowly in cooler water
The sea level there rises by several metres every year
Hurricanes wear the atolls away completely
The hotspot pulls the rock back down
57964.e: The cooled plate slowly sinks as it gets older. Further north the water is cooler, and the corals can no longer make up for the sinking. This limit is called the Darwin Point, after which the atolls become guyots.
57964.m: In the cooler north, corals can no longer make up for the sinking of the atolls.

57965.q: Which volcano on Hawaii destroyed around 700 houses in the Puna district in 2018?
57965.e: During the eruption in Lower Puna, lava flowed for months from fissures in the eastern rift zone of Kīlauea. Over 700 buildings were destroyed.
57965.m: Kīlauea destroyed hundreds of houses in Puna in 2018.

57966.q: How many large caldera-forming eruptions has the Yellowstone volcano had in the last 2.1 million years or so?
57966.e: The three large eruptions formed the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff, the Mesa Falls Tuff and the Lava Creek Tuff. In between there were many smaller lava eruptions.
57966.m: Yellowstone has had three large caldera-forming eruptions in 2.1 million years.

57967.q: How many years ago was the last large Yellowstone eruption that formed today's caldera?
57967.e: The Lava Creek eruption around 630,000 years ago created today's Yellowstone Caldera. Its ash is found across large parts of the USA.
57967.m: Today's Yellowstone Caldera formed around 630,000 years ago.

57968.q: Why is Yellowstone called a supervolcano?
a: Earlier eruptions threw out over 1,000 km³ of material
It erupts several times every year
It is the highest volcano on Earth
57968.e: The largest eruption, around 2.1 million years ago, produced around 2,500 km³ of material. A volcano counts as a supervolcano if it has had an eruption of over 1,000 km³.
57968.m: Supervolcanoes have eruptions of over 1,000 km³ of material.

57969.q: Which landscape in Idaho shows the track the Yellowstone hotspot has left in North America?
57969.e: Because the North American Plate is moving south-west, the volcanic activity seemed to move north-east. The Snake River Plain is a chain of older calderas.
57969.m: The Snake River Plain is the track of the Yellowstone hotspot.

57970.q: What do researchers measure in the Yellowstone Caldera with GPS and satellites?
a: How the ground rises and falls
How many visitors enter the park
How warm the air is in summer
57970.e: Magma and hot fluids deep down make the ground bulge up and sink again in some places. These movements show what is happening inside the volcano.
57970.m: In Yellowstone, the ground rises and falls measurably.

57971.q: According to current measurements, what state is the magma reservoir beneath Yellowstone in?
57971.e: Seismic studies show a reservoir of hot, mostly crystalline rock with melt between the crystals. A major eruption would need much more melt.
57971.m: Beneath Yellowstone lies a hot but mostly solid crystal mush.

57972.q: Which organisation monitors the Yellowstone volcano?
a: NASA with the Mars rover team
57972.e: The Yellowstone Volcano Observatory is a partnership of the US Geological Survey with universities and the National Park. It measures earthquakes, ground movements, gases and temperatures.
57972.m: The USGS monitors Yellowstone with its volcano observatory.

57973.q: Which dangerous event is now considered much more likely in Yellowstone National Park than a supervolcano eruption?
57973.e: In hydrothermal explosions, superheated groundwater suddenly turns to steam and blasts open craters. Such events happen again and again in Yellowstone.
57973.m: In Yellowstone, hydrothermal explosions are much more common than major eruptions.

57974.q: Why do experts think the claim that Yellowstone is “overdue” for a major eruption is wrong?
a: The eruptions follow no fixed rhythm
The hotspot died out long ago
The caldera is filled with water
An eruption would be physically impossible
57974.e: No regular cycle can be worked out from only three major eruptions. An eruption depends on the state of the magma system, not on a calendar.
57974.m: Volcanoes do not follow a fixed eruption rhythm.

57975.q: What speed can pyroclastic flows reach?
57975.e: Pyroclastic flows race downhill as a hot mixture of gas and rock particles. They often reach over 100 km/h, in extreme cases up to around 700 km/h.
57975.m: Pyroclastic flows are far too fast to outrun.

57976.q: What is the rock called that forms from the deposits of large pyroclastic flows?
57976.e: Ignimbrite forms from hot deposits of ash and pumice, which often weld together. The name comes from the Latin ignis for fire and imber for rain, so roughly “fire rain rock”.
57976.m: Pyroclastic flows form the rock ignimbrite.

57977.q: Through which process do pyroclastic flows often form?
a: Through the collapse of an eruption column
Through rain falling on fresh ash
Through lava flowing into the sea
57977.e: If the eruption column becomes too heavy because it takes in too little hot air, it collapses. The material then flows down the flanks as a glowing avalanche.
57977.m: When an eruption column collapses, a pyroclastic flow forms.

57978.q: How did Ludger Sylbaris survive the pyroclastic flow from Mount Pelée in Saint-Pierre in 1902?
a: On a ship far out at sea
57978.e: Sylbaris was in a small, poorly ventilated cell with thick walls. He suffered severe burns but was one of the very few survivors in the town.
57978.m: Ludger Sylbaris survived Mount Pelée in a prison cell.

57979.q: Why can thin, gas-rich glowing clouds from a volcano also spread over hills?
a: They contain a lot of gas and little rock
They are made of liquid lava
They are attracted by the magnetic field
They only flow in river valleys
57979.e: Such glowing clouds are called pyroclastic surges. Because they are lighter and more turbulent than dense pyroclastic flows, they follow the valleys less closely.
57979.m: Gas-rich glowing clouds can also cross hills.

57980.q: Which French expression was coined for pyroclastic flows after the eruption of Mount Pelée in 1902?
57980.e: The geologist Alfred Lacroix described the glowing clouds of Mount Pelée as a “nuée ardente”, meaning burning cloud. The term is still used today.
57980.m: The “nuée ardente” is the burning glowing cloud of a volcano.

57981.q: In which ancient town near Vesuvius were hundreds of skeletons found in boathouses on the beach, killed by pyroclastic flows?
57981.e: In Herculaneum, many people fled to the beach and sheltered in boathouses. The extreme heat of the pyroclastic flows killed them there in the year 79.
57981.m: In Herculaneum, people on the beach died from the heat of pyroclastic flows.

57982.q: Which well-known volcanologists died in a pyroclastic flow at Unzen in Japan in 1991?
57982.e: The Krafft couple from Alsace filmed eruptions from very close up. On 3 June 1991, a total of 43 people died, including the American Harry Glicken.
57982.m: Katia and Maurice Krafft died at Unzen in 1991.

57983.q: Which force drives a pyroclastic flow down the flanks of a volcano?
57983.e: The mixture of gas and rock particles is much denser than the surrounding air. That is why it flows downhill like an avalanche, following gravity.
57983.m: Pyroclastic flows rush downhill like avalanches because of gravity.

57984.q: Roughly how many people died in the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883?
57984.e: Officially, over 36,000 deaths were counted. Most died in the tsunamis on the coasts of Java and Sumatra.
57984.m: The Krakatoa eruption of 1883 killed around 36,000 people.

57985.e: The Sunda Strait separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The tsunamis of 1883 therefore hit the coasts of both islands especially hard.
57985.m: Krakatoa lies in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra.

57986.q: In which month did the eruption of Krakatoa reach its peak in 1883?
57986.e: After months of increased activity, the most violent explosions came on 26 and 27 August 1883. The biggest happened on the morning of 27 August.
57986.m: Krakatoa exploded most violently on 27 August 1883.

57987.q: What value on the Volcanic Explosivity Index did the 1883 Krakatoa eruption reach?
57987.e: Krakatoa threw out around 20 km³ of material, reaching VEI 6. It is one of the largest eruptions of modern times.
57987.m: The Krakatoa eruption of 1883 reached VEI 6.

57988.q: What did barometers around the world record after the biggest Krakatoa explosion?
a: The pressure wave went round the Earth several times
Air pressure stayed high for months
Air pressure dropped to zero everywhere
57988.e: Barographs in many countries recorded the pressure wave, which travelled several times around the whole planet. This was one of the first worldwide measurements of a natural event.
57988.m: Krakatoa's pressure wave went round the Earth several times.

57989.q: What happened to the island of Krakatoa itself in 1883?
a: More than two thirds of the island disappeared
The island grew to twice its size
The island joined up with Java
57989.e: After the magma chamber emptied, over 70 per cent of the island collapsed. A caldera formed, most of which now lies under the sea.
57989.m: In the 1883 eruption, much of the island of Krakatoa sank.

57990.q: In which year did the new volcano Anak Krakatau first rise out of the sea?
57990.e: From 1927, a new volcanic cone grew above sea level on the edge of the caldera. It has been active again and again ever since.
57990.m: Anak Krakatau rose out of the sea in 1927.

57991.q: What triggered a deadly tsunami in the Sunda Strait in December 2018?
a: A flank collapse of Anak Krakatau
57991.e: A large part of Anak Krakatau slid into the sea during an eruption. The tsunami hit the coasts without warning and killed over 400 people.
57991.m: A flank collapse of Anak Krakatau triggered a tsunami in 2018.

57992.q: Which volcanic landform was created in 1883 when the island collapsed over Krakatoa's emptied magma chamber?
57992.e: After the magma chamber emptied, a large part of the island collapsed and a collapse basin, a caldera, formed. What remained was mainly the southern part with the volcano Rakata.
57992.m: A caldera formed in the Krakatoa eruption of 1883.

57993.q: In which year did Mount St. Helens in the north-west of the USA erupt violently?
57993.e: The main eruption began on 18 May 1980. It had been preceded by two months of earthquakes and smaller explosions.

57994.q: Which event started the main eruption of Mount St. Helens in 1980?
a: A huge landslide of the north flank
A lava flow from the summit crater
A lightning strike in the crater
57994.e: An earthquake of magnitude 5.1 triggered the largest landslide in recorded history. This suddenly released the pressure on the magma, which exploded sideways.
57994.m: A huge landslide of the north flank started the 1980 eruption.

57995.q: How many people died in the eruption of Mount St. Helens in 1980?
57995.e: Thanks to exclusion zones, the number of victims was comparatively small. Among the 57 dead was lodge owner Harry R. Truman, who refused to leave his house at Spirit Lake.
57995.m: 57 people died in the eruption of Mount St. Helens.

57996.q: By how much did the 1980 eruption make Mount St. Helens lower?
57996.e: The summit was at around 2,950 m before and around 2,550 m afterwards. In its place a horseshoe-shaped crater remained.
57996.m: Mount St. Helens lost around 400 metres of height in 1980.

57997.q: Which warning sign appeared on the north flank of Mount St. Helens in the weeks before the 1980 eruption?
a: The flank was suddenly free of snow and green
A river of lava flowed out of the flank
The flank sank by several hundred metres
57997.e: Rising magma pushed against the mountain from inside without reaching the surface. As a result, the north flank at times grew outwards by up to 1.5 metres a day.
57997.m: A growing bulge on the flank announced the eruption.

57998.q: Why did comparatively few people die in the eruption of Mount St. Helens in 1980?
a: The area had been declared an exclusion zone beforehand
The eruption happened in the middle of the night
The lava only flowed into the sea
The volcano is on an uninhabited island
57998.e: After weeks of earthquakes and a growing bulge, the authorities closed off the surrounding area. Even so, 57 people died, many of them just outside the exclusion zone.
57998.m: Exclusion zones saved many lives at Mount St. Helens.

57999.q: What does the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measure?
a: How much material an eruption throws out and how violent it is
How hot a volcano's lava is
How many people die in an eruption
57999.e: The VEI ranges from 0 to 8 and mainly takes into account the amount of material thrown out and the height of the eruption column. Each step stands for about ten times more material.
57999.m: The VEI describes how explosive a volcanic eruption is.

58000.q: Which mountain range does Mount St. Helens belong to?
58000.e: The Cascade Range stretches from northern California to British Columbia. It consists of stratovolcanoes such as Mount St. Helens, Mount Rainier and Mount Hood.
58000.m: Mount St. Helens belongs to the volcanic Cascade Range.

58001.q: What have experts especially studied in the protected area around Mount St. Helens since 1980?
a: How plants and animals resettle destroyed land
How to seal volcanoes with concrete
How to get gold from volcanic ash
How glaciers make volcanoes go extinct
58001.e: The eruption left a grey landscape of ash and fallen trees. The area has been protected since 1982, and scientists watch how life returns.
58001.m: At Mount St. Helens you can watch life return.

58002.q: Pinatubo had one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century in 1991. Which country is it in?
58002.e: Pinatubo is on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. Its main eruption in June 1991 threw ash around 35 km high.
58002.m: Pinatubo is a volcano in the Philippines.

58003.q: The 1991 Pinatubo eruption reached a value of 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI). Roughly what does one step more on this scale mean?
a: About ten times more ejected material
58003.e: The VEI is a logarithmic scale: each step stands for about ten times more ejected material. Pinatubo threw out around 10 km³.
58003.m: One VEI step more means about ten times more ejected material.

58004.q: Which gas from the 1991 Pinatubo eruption formed particles in the stratosphere that cooled the climate?
58004.e: Around 15 to 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide turned into sulphate aerosols. These reflected sunlight, and it became about half a degree cooler worldwide.
58004.m: Sulphur dioxide from volcanoes can cool the climate.

58005.q: By how much did the Earth's average temperature temporarily fall after the Pinatubo eruption?
58005.e: The sulphate aerosols reflected part of the sunlight back into space. In 1992 and 1993 it was around 0.5 degrees cooler worldwide.
58005.m: After the Pinatubo eruption it was around half a degree cooler worldwide.

58006.q: Which weather event hit the Philippines at the same time as Pinatubo's main eruption?
58006.e: Typhoon Yunya brought heavy rain, which soaked the ash and made it very heavy. Many roofs collapsed under this weight.
58006.m: Typhoon Yunya made Pinatubo's ash heavy and dangerous.

58007.q: Which large US military base near Pinatubo was evacuated in 1991 and then given up?
58007.e: Clark Air Base was only around 25 km from the volcano and was cleared before the eruption. Because of the severe damage, the USA gave up the base.
58007.m: Clark Air Base was given up after the Pinatubo eruption.

58008.q: On which Philippine island is Pinatubo?
58008.e: Pinatubo lies in the west of Luzon, the largest island of the Philippines, around 90 km north-west of Manila.
58008.m: Pinatubo is on the island of Luzon.

58009.q: Roughly how long had Pinatubo been dormant before 1991?
58009.e: The last major eruption before 1991 had been around 500 years earlier. That is why many people hardly knew the densely forested mountain was a volcano.
58009.m: Before 1991, Pinatubo had been dormant for around 500 years.

58010.q: Why is the forecast of the Pinatubo eruption considered a great success for volcanology?
a: Timely evacuations saved thousands of lives
There was no damage to property at all
58010.e: Philippine and American experts analysed earthquakes and gas measurements and gave early warnings. Tens of thousands of people were brought to safety before the main eruption.
58010.m: The warnings before the Pinatubo eruption saved thousands of lives.

58011.q: What formed in Pinatubo's new caldera after 1991?
58011.e: Monsoon rains gradually filled the caldera, which is around 2.5 km wide, with water. Lake Pinatubo is now also visited by tourists.
58011.m: Today there is a crater lake in Pinatubo's caldera.

58012.q: What does the word “caldera” originally mean?
58012.e: The word comes from Spanish and Portuguese and means cauldron. The geologist Leopold von Buch took it from the Caldera de Taburiente on La Palma.
58012.m: A caldera is a volcanic cauldron.

58013.q: What mainly causes a caldera to form?
a: Collapse over an emptied magma chamber
58013.e: If a large eruption partly empties the magma chamber, the roof above it loses its support. It collapses, forming a basin much larger than a normal crater.
58013.m: A caldera forms when the roof of an emptied magma chamber collapses.

58014.q: Which volcano collapsed around 7,700 years ago and formed today's Crater Lake in Oregon?
58014.e: The eruption of Mount Mazama emptied its magma chamber, after which the summit collapsed. Rain and snow filled the caldera to form Crater Lake, almost 600 m deep.
58014.m: Crater Lake fills the caldera of Mount Mazama.

58015.q: Which Greek island surrounds a caldera that formed in the Minoan eruption around 1600 BC?
58015.e: The Minoan eruption is one of the largest of the last 10,000 years. The caldera is now flooded by the sea, and its steep slopes form the backdrop of Santorini.
58015.m: The island of Santorini frames a flooded caldera.

58016.q: What happens during so-called bradyseism in the Phlegraean Fields near Naples?
a: The ground slowly rises and falls
A glacier slides into the sea
A volcano pours out lava every day
58016.e: In the caldera of the Phlegraean Fields, the ground rises and falls by metres again and again, for example in the harbour town of Pozzuoli. The term comes from Greek and means “slow quake”.
58016.m: Bradyseism raises and lowers the ground of the Phlegraean Fields.

58017.q: Which famous conservation area in Tanzania lies in an extinct caldera?
58017.e: The Ngorongoro Crater is a large, intact caldera around 20 km across. Many large animals live on its floor.
58017.m: The Ngorongoro Crater is a large caldera in Tanzania.

58018.q: What fills the caldera of the Toba supervolcano on Sumatra today?
a: The largest volcanic lake on Earth
58018.e: The Toba supervolcano erupted around 74,000 years ago. Its caldera filled with water to form Lake Toba, the largest volcanic lake in the world. In its middle lies the island of Samosir.
58018.m: Lake Toba fills the caldera of a supervolcano.

58019.q: Which lake in the German Eifel fills a caldera that formed around 13,000 years ago?
58019.e: The Laacher See eruption reached VEI 6, making it one of the largest volcanic eruptions in Central Europe in recent geological history. Its ash is now an important time marker in lake deposits.
58019.m: The Laacher See in the Eifel lies in a caldera.

58020.q: What happened at the summit of Kīlauea in 2018 while lava was coming out far away in Puna?
a: The summit caldera sank in stages
58020.e: As magma drained sideways from the reservoir beneath the summit, the caldera floor sank by hundreds of metres in many stages. Experts were able to watch a caldera form live.
58020.m: In 2018 the summit caldera of Kīlauea sank in stages.

58021.q: What is the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) used for?
a: It compares the strength of explosive eruptions
It predicts when eruptions will happen
It measures the temperature of lava
It counts the active volcanoes in a country
58021.e: The volcanologists Chris Newhall and Stephen Self proposed this standard scale in 1982. It is based mainly on the volume ejected and the height of the eruption column.
58021.m: The VEI compares how explosive volcanic eruptions are.

58022.q: What range of values does the Volcanic Explosivity Index cover?
58022.e: The scale starts at 0 for non-explosive eruptions. Level 8 stands for the largest known eruptions with over 1,000 km³ of material.
58022.m: The Volcanic Explosivity Index ranges from 0 to 8.

58023.q: From VEI 2 upwards, by what factor does the ejected volume grow with each step?
58023.e: The scale is logarithmic. So an eruption of level 6 ejects about ten times more material than one of level 5.
58023.m: Each higher VEI step means about ten times more ejected material.

58024.q: At least how much material must an eruption throw out to reach VEI 8?
58024.e: VEI 8 is the highest level and describes so-called super-eruptions. One example is the eruption of Toba around 74,000 years ago.
58024.m: A VEI 8 eruption throws out more than 1,000 km³ of material.

58025.q: Which eruption of 1815 is the only one in recorded modern history with VEI 7?
58025.e: Tambora on the island of Sumbawa threw out over 100 km³ of material. It is considered the strongest volcanic eruption of the last few centuries.
58025.m: The Tambora eruption of 1815 reached VEI 7.

58026.q: What VEI value did the 2010 eruption of Eyjafjallajökull, which brought European air traffic to a halt, have?
58026.e: In volcanological terms the eruption was rather medium-sized. But the fine ash and the weather over Europe caused massive disruption.
58026.m: The Eyjafjallajökull eruption of 2010 reached VEI 4.

58027.q: Which quantities are mainly used to classify an eruption on the VEI?
a: Ejected volume and height of the eruption column
58027.e: What counts are the volume of ejected tephra and the height of the eruption column. Descriptions such as “gentle” or “violent” are also taken into account.
58027.m: The VEI is based mainly on the ejected volume and the height of the eruption column.

58028.q: Which important quantity does the VEI not take into account, even though it can strongly affect the climate?
a: The height of the eruption column
58028.e: An eruption with a medium VEI can release a great deal of sulphur and cool the climate more than a larger eruption low in sulphur. The VEI only measures explosivity.
58028.m: The VEI says little about an eruption's effect on the climate.

58029.q: What VEI value did the eruption of Vesuvius in the year 79, which buried Pompeii, have?
58029.e: Vesuvius threw out a few cubic kilometres of material and formed a Plinian eruption column over 30 km high. That corresponds to VEI 5.
58029.m: The eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 reached VEI 5.

58030.q: Which seismologist developed a well-known scale for the strength of earthquakes in 1935 together with Beno Gutenberg?
58030.e: Charles Richter and Beno Gutenberg developed the scale at the California Institute of Technology. Today it is known as the Richter scale.
58030.m: The Richter scale is named after Charles Richter.

58031.q: For which region was the Richter scale originally calibrated?
58031.e: The formula was calibrated with earthquakes from Southern California. It has to be adjusted for other regions.
58031.m: Strictly speaking, the original Richter scale only applies to Southern California.

58032.q: What does the Richter scale give?
a: The magnitude, calculated from the swing on the seismogram
The length of the earthquake in seconds
The depth of the earthquake focus
58032.e: The Richter magnitude is calculated from the largest swing of a seismograph. The damage, by contrast, is described by an intensity scale such as the Mercalli scale.
58032.m: The Richter scale measures the strength of an earthquake, not the damage.

58033.q: By what factor is the swing on the seismogram larger at magnitude 6 than at magnitude 5?
58033.e: The Richter scale is logarithmic: one step more means a swing about ten times larger. The energy released even rises by around 30 times.
58033.m: One step more on the Richter scale means about ten times more swing.

58034.q: Which scale is now mostly used for very strong earthquakes, because the Richter scale becomes inaccurate there?
58034.e: In strong earthquakes, the swings hardly grow any more with the strength of the quake: the Richter scale saturates. The moment magnitude is based on the size of the rupture area and the slip.
58034.m: Strong earthquakes are given as moment magnitude.

58035.q: What does the magnitude of an earthquake give?
a: The energy released at the focus
The damage to buildings at one place
The depth of the earthquake focus
58035.e: The magnitude describes the strength of the earthquake at its focus and is a single value for each earthquake. The damage at one place, by contrast, is described by the intensity.
58035.m: Magnitude measures the strength of an earthquake at its focus.

58036.q: What does the intensity of an earthquake describe, for example on the Mercalli scale?
a: The effects at a particular place
The size of the rupture area
58036.e: Intensity is worked out from observations, for example whether people feel the earthquake or buildings are damaged. An earthquake therefore has different intensities at different places but only one magnitude.
58036.m: Intensity shows how strongly an earthquake is felt at a place.

58037.q: Why is the strength of large earthquakes now usually given as moment magnitude?
a: It does not underestimate even very strong earthquakes
It can be worked out without instruments
It only applies to earthquakes in Europe
It measures the damage to buildings
58037.e: Older scales such as the Richter scale reach an upper limit for very strong earthquakes and underestimate them. The moment magnitude is based on the size of the rupture at the focus and stays meaningful even for giant earthquakes.
58037.m: Moment magnitude stays meaningful even for giant earthquakes.

58038.q: Roughly how much more energy does a magnitude 8 earthquake release than a magnitude 6 one?
58038.e: With each magnitude step, the energy rises by a factor of around 32. Two steps make about 32 times 32, so around 1,000.
58038.m: Two magnitude steps mean about a thousand times more energy.

58039.q: Roughly what moment magnitude is the Basel earthquake of 1356 given today?
58039.e: The Swiss Seismological Service assumes a magnitude of around 6.6 for the Basel earthquake; older and newer estimates range from about 6 to 7. It is considered the strongest historically documented earthquake in Central Europe.
58039.m: The Basel earthquake of 1356 had a magnitude of about 6.6.

a: The distance between the epicentre and the measuring station
The depth of the earthquake focus
The length of the ruptured fault
58040.e: The epicentral distance is the distance from the measuring station to the epicentre on the Earth's surface. For distant earthquakes it is often given in degrees.
58040.m: The epicentral distance is the distance from the station to the epicentre.

58041.q: A station measures 20 seconds between the P wave and the S wave (vP 6 km/s, vS 3.5 km/s). How far away is the epicentre?
58041.e: d/3.5 minus d/6 equals 20 s, so d times 0.119 equals 20. This gives d equals around 168 km.
58041.m: You can work out the distance to an earthquake from the time gap between the P and S waves.

58042.q: A station is at an epicentral distance of 30 degrees from the earthquake. Roughly how many kilometres is that?
58042.e: One degree of the Earth's circumference is around 111 km. 30 times 111 km makes about 3,330 km.
58042.m: One degree of epicentral distance is about 111 kilometres.

58043.q: What are lines of equal earthquake intensity drawn on a map around the epicentre called?
58043.e: Isoseismals connect places where an earthquake was felt equally strongly. In the past, the epicentre of historical earthquakes was estimated from the innermost isoseismal.
58043.m: Isoseismals connect places of equal earthquake intensity.

58044.q: Why is the greatest damage in very strong earthquakes often far from the epicentre?
a: The rupture continues for hundreds of kilometres
The waves are swallowed at the epicentre
There are never buildings at the epicentre
The epicentre is always in the sea
58044.e: The epicentre only marks the point above where the rupture began. In great earthquakes the rupture continues over a long distance and causes strong shaking all along the fault.
58044.m: The epicentre only shows where the rupture began.

58045.q: Which technical term is used to mean the same as hypocentre?
58045.e: The hypocentre is also called the earthquake focus. It is the point inside the Earth where the rupture begins.
58045.m: The hypocentre is also called the focus.

58046.q: Where do earthquakes with foci several hundred kilometres below the surface mainly occur?
a: In sinking plates at subduction zones
In the middle of stable continents
58046.e: Deep-focus earthquakes from around 300 km down occur almost only where a cold, brittle plate sinks into the mantle, for example beneath Japan or the Andes.
58046.m: Deep-focus earthquakes happen in sinking plates.

58047.q: Roughly down to what depth do the deepest known earthquakes occur?
58047.e: The deepest earthquakes happen in sinking lithospheric plates down to a depth of around 700 km. Below that the rock is too plastic for brittle fractures.
58047.m: Below about 700 kilometres there are no more earthquakes.

58048.q: Why do shallow earthquakes usually cause more damage than deep ones of the same magnitude?
a: The waves travel a shorter distance
Deep earthquakes produce no S waves
58048.e: The closer the focus is to the surface, the less the waves are weakened on their way. The shaking at the ground is therefore stronger.
58048.m: Shallow earthquakes are usually more destructive than deep ones.

58049.q: A focus is 30 km deep and the station is 40 km from the epicentre. What is the hypocentral distance?
58049.e: The focal depth and the epicentral distance form the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle. The square root of 30² plus 40², that is of 2,500, gives 50 km.
58049.m: You calculate the hypocentral distance with Pythagoras' theorem.

58050.q: How do the rock particles move in a P wave?
a: Back and forth in the direction of travel
At right angles to the direction of travel
58050.e: P waves are longitudinal or compression waves. The rock is alternately squeezed and stretched, similar to sound.
58050.m: P waves are pressure waves like sound waves.

58051.q: Roughly what speed does a P wave have in the Earth's crust?
58051.e: In the crust, P waves travel at around 5 to 7 km/s. In the mantle they become even faster with increasing depth.
58051.m: P waves travel about six kilometres per second in the Earth's crust.

58052.q: What causes the P-wave shadow zone between about 103 and 142 degrees of epicentral distance?
a: Refraction at the liquid outer core
58052.e: At the core-mantle boundary, the P-wave speed drops sharply. The waves are refracted and do not reach this part of the surface directly.
58052.m: The Earth's core bends P waves and so creates a shadow zone.

58053.q: Which seismologist discovered the solid inner core in 1936 using P waves?
58053.e: The Dane Inge Lehmann interpreted weak P-wave signals in the shadow zone as reflections from an inner core. This showed that the Earth's core consists of two parts.
58053.m: Inge Lehmann discovered the inner core in 1936.

58054.q: What did Andrija Mohorovičić discover in 1909 from a jump in wave speed?
a: The boundary between crust and mantle
The boundary between mantle and core
58054.e: After an earthquake in Croatia, he noticed two groups of P waves. He concluded that the speed suddenly increases at a boundary deep down, the so-called Moho.
58054.m: The Moho separates the Earth's crust from the mantle.

58055.q: What are earthquake early warning systems, such as in Japan, based on?
a: They detect the fast P wave before the destructive waves
They measure gas leaks days before the earthquake
They calculate earthquakes from the phase of the moon
58055.e: The P wave is faster but does little damage. If it is detected near the focus, trains can be braked and people warned before the stronger waves arrive.
58055.m: Early warning systems use the head start of the P wave.

58056.q: What kind of wave is an S wave?
58056.e: In S waves, the particles move at right angles to the direction of travel. The rock is sheared, not squeezed.

58057.q: Roughly how fast is an S wave compared with a P wave in the same rock?
58057.e: In typical rock, the S-wave speed is around the P-wave speed divided by the square root of 3, so about 58 per cent.
58057.m: S waves are much slower than P waves.

58058.q: What was concluded from the fact that no direct S waves arrive beyond about 103 degrees?
a: The crust is thin under the oceans
58058.e: Direct S waves are missing on the opposite side of the Earth. This shows that they cannot pass through a layer with no shear strength: the liquid outer core.
58058.m: The S-wave shadow proves that the outer core is liquid.

58059.q: At what depth did Beno Gutenberg determine the boundary between the mantle and the core in 1914?
58059.e: From the travel times of earthquake waves, Gutenberg calculated a core boundary at a depth of around 2,900 km. Today it is called the Gutenberg discontinuity.
58059.m: The core-mantle boundary lies at a depth of about 2,900 kilometres.

58060.q: Why do S waves usually cause more damage to buildings than P waves?
a: They have larger amplitudes and shake sideways
They are faster than all other waves
They produce great heat in the ground
58060.e: S waves move the ground back and forth sideways with bigger swings. Many buildings are poorly protected against such sideways forces.
58060.m: S waves shake buildings sideways and are therefore more dangerous than P waves.

58061.q: What are the two types of surface waves that arrive after the P and S waves called?
58061.e: Surface waves form when body waves reach the surface. Love waves move horizontally, Rayleigh waves on elliptical paths.
58061.m: Love and Rayleigh waves travel along the Earth's surface.

58062.q: In which direction does the San Andreas Fault move the two sides against each other?
58062.e: If you stand on one side of the fault, the opposite side moves to the right. This is called a dextral strike-slip fault.
58062.m: The San Andreas Fault is a right-lateral strike-slip fault.

58063.q: Which plate lies west of the San Andreas Fault?
58063.e: West of the fault lies the Pacific Plate, which moves north-west relative to the North American Plate. That is why Los Angeles and San Diego belong to the Pacific Plate.
58063.m: The Pacific Plate lies west of the San Andreas Fault.

58064.q: Roughly how long is the San Andreas Fault?
58064.e: The fault runs for around 1,200 km through California, from Cape Mendocino in the north to the Salton Sea in the south.
58064.m: The San Andreas Fault is around 1,200 kilometres long.

58065.q: Into which structure does the San Andreas Fault pass in the south near the Salton Sea?
a: Into the spreading zone of the Gulf of California
Into the deep-sea trench off Chile
58065.e: At its southern end, the transform fault passes into a system of short spreading axes in the Gulf of California. There the gulf is slowly opening.
58065.m: In the south, the San Andreas Fault passes into the Gulf of California.

58066.q: Which big city on the San Andreas Fault was badly destroyed in 1906 by an earthquake and the fires that followed?
58066.e: The 1906 earthquake and the fires afterwards destroyed large parts of San Francisco. The city lies only a few kilometres from the fault.
58066.m: San Francisco was destroyed in 1906 by an earthquake on the San Andreas Fault.

58067.q: What was the maximum horizontal offset in the San Francisco earthquake of 1906?
58067.e: In the earthquake, with a magnitude of around 7.8 to 7.9, fences and roads along the fault were shifted by up to about 6 m.
58067.m: The 1906 earthquake shifted the ground by several metres.

58068.q: Why do experts expect an especially strong earthquake in the south of the San Andreas Fault?
a: The section has been locked for over 150 years and has built up a lot of stress
The fault there constantly slides slowly
One plate sinks beneath the other there
There is an active hotspot there
58068.e: Since the last great earthquake in 1857, the southern section has hardly moved. The built-up stress could be released in an earthquake often called “The Big One”.
58068.m: Locked sections of a fault store stress for big earthquakes.

58069.q: Why has the village of Parkfield on the San Andreas Fault been monitored especially closely since the 1980s?
a: Moderate earthquakes happened there at strikingly regular intervals
The deepest point of the fault is there
The great earthquake of 1906 started there
58069.e: Since 1857, Parkfield has had repeated earthquakes of around magnitude 6. The USGS hoped to predict and measure the next one precisely; it only came in 2004.
58069.m: Parkfield is an open-air laboratory for earthquake research.

58070.q: Why did researchers drill deep into the San Andreas Fault from 2004 onwards?
a: To study the rock and processes directly in the fault
To stop the fault with concrete
To get groundwater for Los Angeles
58070.e: In the SAFOD project, a borehole was drilled into the active fault zone. This made it possible to study rock and place instruments directly in the fault.
58070.m: Deep drilling helps to study earthquakes right at the fault.

58071.q: What is the effect when a section of the San Andreas Fault slides slowly and almost continuously?
a: Less stress builds up for big earthquakes
58071.e: Some sections in central California creep a little all the time. Less stress builds up there, while locked sections release it suddenly in big earthquakes.
58071.m: Creeping sections slide slowly without causing big earthquakes.

58072.q: On which date did the Tōhoku earthquake happen?
58072.e: The earthquake began on 11 March 2011 at 14:46 local time off the coast of Miyagi Prefecture.
58072.m: The Tōhoku earthquake happened on 11 March 2011.

58073.q: What moment magnitude did the Tōhoku earthquake have?
58073.e: The Japan Meteorological Agency gives 9.0, the USGS 9.1. It was the strongest earthquake ever measured in Japan.
58073.m: At a magnitude of around 9, the Tōhoku earthquake was Japan's strongest earthquake.

58074.q: At which deep-sea trench did the Tōhoku earthquake occur?
58074.e: At the Japan Trench, the Pacific Plate sinks beneath north-east Japan at around 8 cm per year. There the built-up stress was released in the megaquake.
58074.m: The Tōhoku earthquake occurred at the Japan Trench.

58075.q: What was the greatest run-up height of the 2011 tsunami on the Japanese coast?
58075.e: In the city of Miyako in Iwate Prefecture, a run-up height of around 40.5 m was measured. That is the highest value ever measured in Japan.
58075.m: On some coasts the 2011 tsunami ran up around 40 metres high.

58076.q: By how much was the main island of Honshū moved east by the 2011 earthquake?
58076.e: GPS measurements showed that parts of Honshū moved around 2.4 m to the east. The coast also sank in places.
58076.m: The earthquake moved parts of Japan by several metres.

58077.q: According to calculations, how did the Tōhoku earthquake change the length of the day?
58077.e: Because mass was shifted, the Earth spins very slightly faster. The effect can be measured but makes no difference in everyday life.
58077.m: Big earthquakes can change the Earth's rotation very slightly.

58078.q: Which event came before the Tōhoku main earthquake on 9 March 2011?
58078.e: Two days before the main earthquake, an earthquake of magnitude 7.2 happened around 40 km away. Only afterwards was it recognised as a foreshock.
58078.m: Strong earthquakes can have foreshocks that are only recognised later.

58079.q: By what name is the 2011 disaster known in Japan?
58079.e: In Japan the disaster is called Higashi-Nihon daishinsai, the Great East Japan Earthquake. The Kantō earthquake was in 1923, the Hanshin earthquake in 1995.
58079.m: The Japanese call the 2011 disaster the Great East Japan Earthquake.

58080.q: Roughly how many dead and missing did the 2011 disaster cause?
58080.e: Officially, around 19,800 dead and just over 2,500 missing are counted (as of 2021). Most died in the tsunami.
58080.m: In the Tōhoku earthquake, most people died in the tsunami.

58081.q: Roughly how high was the tsunami that destroyed the emergency power supply at Fukushima Daiichi in 2011?
58081.e: The wave reached around 14 to 15 m at the power station and flooded the emergency generators. As a result, the cooling of the reactors failed.
58081.m: The tsunami flooded the power station's emergency power supply.

58082.q: What moment magnitude is given to the Indian Ocean undersea earthquake of 2004?
58082.e: The USGS gives 9.1, and some researchers estimated up to 9.3. It is one of the three strongest earthquakes ever recorded.
58082.m: The 2004 undersea earthquake is one of the strongest earthquakes ever measured.

58083.q: Which plates were involved in the 2004 undersea earthquake?
a: Indian Plate beneath the Eurasian Plate
Pacific Plate beneath the Philippine Plate
African Plate beneath the Arabian Plate
Australian Plate beneath the Pacific Plate
58083.e: At the Sunda Trench, the Indo-Australian Plate pushes beneath the Eurasian Plate (Burma microplate) by a few centimetres per year.
58083.m: The 2004 earthquake happened because the Indian Plate sinks beneath Eurasia.

58084.q: Roughly how long was the rupture zone of the 2004 earthquake?
58084.e: The rupture ran for more than 1,000 km from northern Sumatra to the Andaman Islands and lasted several minutes.
58084.m: The 2004 rupture zone was over a thousand kilometres long.

58085.q: Roughly how many people died altogether in the 2004 undersea earthquake and tsunami?
58085.e: About 230,000 people lost their lives in around a dozen countries. It is one of the deadliest tsunamis in history.

58086.q: Which country had the most deaths in the 2004 tsunami?
58086.e: In Indonesia alone, well over 100,000 people died, most of them in Aceh province near the epicentre.
58086.m: Indonesia was hit hardest by the 2004 tsunami.

58087.q: Which city in the north of Sumatra was especially badly destroyed in 2004?
58087.e: Banda Aceh lies at the northern tip of Sumatra near the epicentre. The waves reached the coast of Aceh only about 20 minutes after the earthquake and caused devastating damage there.
58087.m: Banda Aceh was almost wiped out by the 2004 tsunami.

58088.q: Which African country had the most tsunami victims in 2004?
58088.e: The tsunami crossed the whole Indian Ocean. In Somalia several hundred people died, and the village of Hafun was largely destroyed.
58088.m: The 2004 tsunami even claimed victims in East Africa.

58089.q: Roughly how long did the 2004 tsunami take to reach the coast of Sri Lanka?
58089.e: The waves travelled around 1,600 km and arrived about two hours after the earthquake. A warning system could have given time to evacuate.
58089.m: A tsunami can cross an ocean in a few hours.

58090.q: What was set up in the Indian Ocean after the 2004 tsunami that did not exist there before?
a: A network of underwater power stations
58090.e: Before 2004 there was no tsunami warning system in the Indian Ocean. Afterwards, the countries around it built one with international help, including a German-Indonesian system that started operating in 2008.
58090.m: After 2004, a tsunami warning system was set up in the Indian Ocean.

58091.q: Why did very few people die on the island of Simeulue near the epicentre in 2004?
a: A traditional warning, “smong”, made them flee
The island was sheltered from the wind
A dam held back the waves
58091.e: After a tsunami in 1907, the islanders passed on the rule to flee inland at once after an earthquake when the sea draws back. That is how almost everyone survived.
58091.m: Knowledge passed down the generations can save lives in natural disasters.

58092.q: What moment magnitude did the 2010 Haiti earthquake have?
58092.e: The USGS determined a magnitude of 7.0. Despite its comparatively medium strength, it was one of the deadliest earthquakes in history.
58092.m: The 2010 Haiti earthquake had a magnitude of 7.0.

58093.q: Where was the epicentre of the 2010 Haiti earthquake?
58093.e: The epicentre was near Léogâne, only around 25 km from the capital. The focus was also only about 13 km deep.
58093.m: In the Haiti earthquake, the epicentre was near the capital.

58094.q: On which large fault zone in the south of Haiti did the 2010 earthquake happen?
58094.e: The earthquake happened in the Enriquillo-Plantain Garden fault zone, a left-lateral strike-slip fault. Later studies showed that it was mainly hidden side faults that ruptured.
58094.m: The Haiti earthquake happened on the Enriquillo-Plantain Garden fault zone.

58095.q: On the boundary of which two plates does Haiti lie?
58095.e: The Caribbean Plate moves east relative to the North American Plate by around 2 cm per year. The boundary zone runs right across Hispaniola.
58095.m: Haiti lies on the boundary between the Caribbean and North American Plates.

58096.q: What made the Haiti earthquake so devastating?
a: Shallow focus, closeness to the capital and unsafe buildings
A volcanic eruption at the same time
A giant tsunami over the whole island
58096.e: The shallow earthquake hit the densely populated capital almost directly. Many houses had been built without earthquake protection and collapsed.
58096.m: How buildings are built often decides the number of victims.

58097.q: What death toll did Haiti's government give one year after the earthquake?
58097.e: Prime Minister Bellerive spoke of around 316,000 dead. Other estimates are lower, and the exact figure is still uncertain today.
58097.m: The number of victims in Haiti in 2010 is still disputed today.

58098.q: Roughly how many people were made homeless by the 2010 Haiti earthquake?
58098.e: Estimates put the number of homeless at around 1.5 million, and many lived in tent camps for a long time. Altogether around a third of the population was affected.
58098.m: After the earthquake, well over a million people in Haiti were left without a home.

58099.q: Which famous building in Port-au-Prince largely collapsed in 2010?
58099.e: The presidential palace, the National Palace, largely collapsed. The cathedral and many ministries were also destroyed.
58099.m: The 2010 earthquake also destroyed Haiti's presidential palace.

58100.q: Which organisation suffered the heaviest loss in the history of its peacekeeping missions in the 2010 Haiti earthquake?
58100.e: The headquarters of the UN stabilisation mission in Port-au-Prince collapsed. Around 100 UN staff died, including the head of the mission.
58100.m: The Haiti earthquake was the heaviest loss in the history of UN peacekeeping missions.

58101.q: Which epidemic broke out in October 2010 in Haiti, already weakened by the earthquake?
58101.e: Cholera began in the Artibonite region and spread quickly. In 2016 the UN admitted partial responsibility, because the germ had probably been brought in by peacekeepers.
58101.m: After the earthquake, Haiti also suffered a cholera epidemic.

58102.q: Which physical principle is a classic mechanical seismograph based on?
a: The inertia of a suspended mass
The air pressure in a chamber
58102.e: When the ground shakes, the casing moves with the ground, while the heavy mass stays almost still because of its inertia. The relative movement is recorded.
58102.m: A seismograph uses the inertia of a mass.

58103.q: What is the difference between a seismometer and a seismograph?
a: The seismometer measures, the seismograph also records
There is no difference in technical language
58103.e: The seismometer is the sensor for ground movement. Together with a recording unit it makes a seismograph, which produces a seismogram.
58103.m: A seismograph measures and records ground movements.

58104.q: Why do modern seismometer stations have three measuring components?
a: To record north-south, east-west and vertical movement
To measure three different earthquakes at once
To separate P, S and surface waves
To cover day, night and weekends
58104.e: Ground movements happen in all directions. With three sensors at right angles to each other, the complete movement can be reconstructed.
58104.m: A three-component seismometer measures movements in all three directions.

58105.q: In which country did modern seismology develop especially early because of the many earthquakes in the late 19th century?
58105.e: Researchers such as the Briton John Milne built sensitive seismographs in Tokyo. Japan thus became a centre of early earthquake research.
58105.m: Japan was an early centre of earthquake research.

58107.q: What did Ernst von Rebeur-Paschwitz record for the first time in Potsdam in 1889?
58107.e: His horizontal pendulum recorded waves from an earthquake in Japan. This proved for the first time that earthquake waves travel through the whole globe.
58107.m: Since 1889 we have known that distant earthquakes can be measured worldwide.

58108.q: What does the word “seismograph” literally mean in Greek?
58108.e: It is made up of “seismos” for shaking and “graphein” for writing.

58109.q: What is special about a broadband seismometer?
a: It records very slow to fast ground vibrations
It only measures earthquakes above magnitude 8
58109.e: Broadband instruments measure vibrations with periods from fractions of a second to several hundred seconds. This means near and distant earthquakes can be analysed equally well.
58109.m: Broadband seismometers measure a very wide range of frequencies.

58110.q: Which instrument is used near the focus so that very strong ground movements do not overload it?
58110.e: Sensitive seismometers reach their limits in strong shaking. Strong-motion instruments measure ground acceleration even in severe earthquakes, for example for earthquake-proof buildings.
58110.m: Strong ground movements are measured with accelerometers.

58111.q: Apart from earthquake research, what task does a worldwide network of seismometers carry out?
58111.e: Underground nuclear explosions produce ground waves like small earthquakes. The international monitoring system for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty therefore uses seismometers all over the world.
58111.m: Seismometers can also detect nuclear tests.

58112.q: Why does an oceanic plate sink beneath a continental plate when they collide?
a: It is thicker than the continental plate
58112.e: Oceanic lithosphere made of basalt is denser than continental crust. That is why it sinks into the Earth's mantle.
58112.m: The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the lighter continental one.

58113.q: What are the extremely strong thrust earthquakes at the boundary of a subduction zone called?
58113.e: At the locked boundary between the plates, stress builds up over centuries. When it is released, the strongest earthquakes on Earth happen.
58113.m: The strongest earthquakes are megathrust earthquakes at subduction zones.

58114.q: What is the wedge of scraped-off sediments at the edge of the upper plate called?
58114.e: As the plate sinks, sediments are scraped off the lower plate and added to the upper plate. In this way an accretionary wedge grows.
58114.m: Scraped-off sediments form an accretionary wedge at subduction zones.

58115.q: What happens when two continental plates collide?
a: A fold mountain range is piled up
One plate sinks deep into the mantle
58115.e: Continental crust is too light to sink deep. So the plates are compressed and pile up a fold mountain range, such as the Himalayas.
58115.m: When two continents collide, a fold mountain range forms.

58116.q: What happens to rock that gets to great depth in a subduction zone?
a: It is turned into new rock by high pressure
It is ground into loose sand
58116.e: Under high pressure and high temperature, new minerals form in the rock; this is called metamorphism. Typical of subduction zones is blueschist, which forms at high pressure and fairly low temperature.
58116.m: In subduction zones, rock is transformed by high pressure.

58117.q: How was the Cascadia earthquake of 1700 on the north-west coast of America dated precisely?
a: From Japanese records of a tsunami with no earthquake felt
From the diaries of Spanish sailors
From radiocarbon dating to the exact day
From measurements by an early seismograph
58117.e: In January 1700 a tsunami was recorded in Japan without the ground shaking there. Together with dead forests on the coast of North America, the earthquake could be dated to 26 January 1700.
58117.m: A tsunami can give away a distant earthquake.

58118.q: Why do subduction earthquakes trigger tsunamis especially often?
a: The sea floor is suddenly lifted
The Earth's rotation suddenly slows down
The moon pulls more strongly after the earthquake
58118.e: The upper plate is bent over years and springs back during the earthquake. The sea floor rises and pushes away the whole column of water above it.
58118.m: A suddenly lifted sea floor sets off a tsunami.

58119.q: Which force of the sinking plate is considered an important driver of plate movement?
58119.e: The cold, dense plate sinks into the mantle and pulls the rest of the plate along behind it. This slab pull is considered one of the strongest driving forces.
58119.m: The sinking plate pulls the rest of the plate along with it.

58120.q: At what time of day did the first main earthquake in Turkey and Syria happen on 6 February 2023?
58120.e: The earthquake hit people in their sleep at 4:17 local time. Many were buried in their homes, and it was also cold winter weather.
58120.m: The earthquake of 6 February 2023 happened in the middle of the night.

58121.q: What moment magnitude did the first main earthquake in Turkey on 6 February 2023 have?
58121.e: The earthquake near Kahramanmaraş reached a magnitude of 7.8. It was one of the strongest earthquakes in Turkey since measurements began.
58121.m: The first earthquake of 6 February 2023 had a magnitude of 7.8.

58122.q: What was especially unusual about the 2023 earthquake in Turkey and Syria?
a: Around 9 hours later a second earthquake above magnitude 7 followed
It triggered an eruption of Mount Ararat
It lasted over an hour without a break
It was not measured in Europe
58122.e: In the afternoon a separate earthquake of magnitude 7.5 to 7.7 followed near Elbistan on a neighbouring fault. This greatly increased the destruction.
58122.m: On 6 February 2023 two very strong earthquakes happened on the same day.

58123.q: On which fault did the main earthquake of 2023 happen?
58123.e: The East Anatolian Fault is a left-lateral strike-slip fault. The rupture stretched over around 350 km.
58123.m: The 2023 earthquake happened on the East Anatolian Fault.

58124.q: Which plate pushes from the south against the Anatolian Plate and drives the movement on the fault?
58124.e: The Arabian Plate is moving north against Eurasia. This squeezes the Anatolian Plate out sideways to the west.
58124.m: The Arabian Plate pushes Anatolia westwards.

58125.q: How many deaths did the 2023 earthquakes in Turkey and Syria cause altogether?
58125.e: Around 59,000 to 62,000 people died, over 53,000 of them in Turkey and several thousand in Syria.
58125.m: The 2023 earthquake was one of Turkey's worst disasters.

58126.q: After which province near the epicentre is the 2023 earthquake series often named?
58126.e: The epicentre of the first earthquake was near Pazarcık in Kahramanmaraş province. That is why it is also called the Kahramanmaraş earthquake.
58126.m: The 2023 earthquake series is named after Kahramanmaraş.

58127.q: Which historic city, ancient Antioch, was badly destroyed in 2023?
58127.e: Antakya in Hatay province was devastated over a large area. Historic churches and mosques also collapsed.
58127.m: Ancient Antioch is called Antakya today.

58128.q: Which earlier rule was strongly criticised in public after the 2023 earthquake?
a: A building amnesty for unapproved buildings
A ban on building near the coast
58128.e: In 2018, owners could have unapproved buildings legalised for a fee. Critics saw this as one reason for poor earthquake safety.
58128.m: Good building rules only help if they are actually followed.

58129.q: Which Swiss organisation sent a search and rescue team to Turkey in 2023?
58129.e: Swiss Rescue sent 87 specialists with search dogs to Hatay province. It includes the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), Redog and army rescue troops, among others.
58129.m: Swiss Rescue helps after earthquakes all over the world.

58130.q: What forms at a divergent plate boundary in the ocean?
58130.e: The plates move apart, rising magma fills the gap and hardens into new oceanic crust. In this way the sea floor keeps growing.
58130.m: New sea floor forms at divergent plate boundaries.

58131.q: Which process mainly produces the magma at mid-ocean ridges?
58131.e: Hot mantle rock rises, the pressure drops and the rock starts to melt partly without any heat being added. This is called decompression melting.
58131.m: When the pressure on hot mantle drops, it partly melts.

58132.q: Which typical form of lava develops when basaltic lava comes out on the sea floor?
58132.e: In cold seawater, the surface of the lava hardens at once, and rounded, pillow-shaped bodies form. Pillow lava is typical of the ocean floor.
58132.m: Under water, basalt lava hardens into pillow lava.

58133.q: Which observation on the sea floor supported the theory of sea-floor spreading in the 1960s?
a: Symmetrical magnetic stripes on both sides of the ridges
Rocks of the same age across the whole ocean
Thick sediments right on the ridges
Granite as the main rock of the ocean floor
58133.e: On both sides of the ridges, the rocks show mirror-image stripes of normal and reversed magnetisation. Vine, Matthews and Morley interpreted this as a record of pole reversals in newly formed crust.
58133.m: The magnetic stripes on the sea floor are mirror images on both sides of the ridge.

58134.q: How does the age of the oceanic crust change with increasing distance from the mid-ocean ridge?
58134.e: The youngest crust forms at the ridge and is then pushed away to the sides. The further away, the older the sea floor.
58134.m: The further from the ridge, the older the ocean floor.

58135.q: What are hot springs on spreading ridges that give out dark, mineral-rich water called?
58135.e: Seawater seeps into the crust, is heated strongly and dissolves metal sulphides. When it comes out, these settle out and colour the water black.
58135.m: Black smokers are hot springs on the sea floor.

58136.q: Which name is another technical term for a divergent plate boundary?
58136.e: Because new lithosphere is built there, it is called constructive. Subduction zones are destructive, transform faults are conservative.
58136.m: Divergent plate boundaries build crust and are therefore called constructive.

58137.q: Which mid-ocean ridge is one of the fastest spreading on Earth?
58137.e: At the East Pacific Rise, more than 10 centimetres of new sea floor form per year in places. The Gakkel Ridge in the Arctic Ocean, by contrast, is one of the slowest.
58137.m: The East Pacific Rise spreads especially fast.

58138.q: Which US geologist published the model of sea-floor spreading in 1962?
58138.e: Harry Hess described how magma rises at the ridges and pushes the sea floor away to the sides. The model became a building block of plate tectonics.
58138.m: Harry Hess explained how the sea floor spreads.

58139.q: Why does the oceanic plate sink when an oceanic plate collides with a continental one?
58139.e: Oceanic lithosphere made of basalt is denser than the lighter continental crust. So it sinks into the mantle, which is called subduction.
58139.m: The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the lighter continental plate.

58140.q: Which landform develops on the sea floor where a plate is subducted?
58140.e: Where the oceanic plate bends downwards, a long, very deep trench forms. The deepest is the Mariana Trench.
58140.m: There is a deep-sea trench in front of every subduction zone.

58141.q: How are the earthquake foci at a subduction zone distributed at depth?
a: All just below the Earth's surface
Scattered at random with no pattern
58141.e: The earthquake foci follow the sinking plate at a slant down to a depth of around 700 kilometres. This zone is called the Wadati-Benioff zone.
58141.m: Earthquake foci trace the slanting path of the sinking plate.

58142.q: What forms when an oceanic plate sinks beneath another oceanic plate?
58142.e: The magma from the subduction zone rises and forms an arc-shaped chain of volcanic islands. Examples are the Marianas and the Lesser Antilles.

58143.q: What is the body of sediments called that is scraped off the sinking plate and piled up at a subduction zone?
58143.e: The top layer of sediment on the sinking plate is scraped off against the upper plate and stacked in a wedge. In this way the edge of the continent grows over time.
58143.m: Scraped-off sediments form an accretionary wedge at subduction zones.

58144.q: Why does magma form above a sinking plate?
a: Released water lowers the melting point of the mantle
The plate melts completely through friction
The pressure in the mantle drops sharply
Heat from the sun reaches deep down
58144.e: Deep down, the sinking plate releases water. This rises into the mantle wedge above and lowers the melting point of the rock there.
58144.m: Water from the sinking plate makes the mantle above it melt.

58145.q: What is the force called with which a sinking, heavy plate pulls the rest of the plate along behind it?
58145.e: The cold, dense lithosphere sinks into the mantle and drags the plate after it. Slab pull is considered the most important driving force of plate tectonics.
58145.m: Slab pull is the most important driving force of plate movement.

58146.q: Why are rocks at subduction zones transformed at high pressure but relatively low temperature?
a: The cold plate sinks quickly to great depth
There is no geothermal heat at all in subduction zones
The rocks there lie right at the surface
58146.e: The cold oceanic plate quickly gets to great depth without warming up much. This creates special rocks such as blueschist.
58146.m: At subduction zones there is high pressure at comparatively low temperature.

58147.q: Roughly how deep is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench?
58147.e: The Challenger Deep reaches almost 11,000 metres below sea level. It is the deepest known point in the oceans.
58147.m: The deepest point of the oceans is around 11 kilometres below the sea surface.

58148.q: What happens to the Earth's crust at a transform fault?
a: It is neither created nor destroyed
It is sunk into the mantle
58148.e: The plates slide sideways past each other. That is why such boundaries are also called conservative.
58148.m: At transform faults, plates slide sideways past each other.

58149.q: Between which plates does the San Andreas Fault run?
a: Juan de Fuca and Pacific Plates
58149.e: In California, the San Andreas Fault separates the Pacific Plate from the North American Plate. It is one of the best-known transform faults on land.
58149.m: The San Andreas Fault separates the Pacific and North American Plates.

58150.q: On which plate is the city of Los Angeles?
58150.e: Los Angeles lies west of the San Andreas Fault and therefore on the Pacific Plate. It is slowly moving north-west towards San Francisco.
58150.m: Los Angeles is on the Pacific Plate.

58151.q: Which devastating earthquake of 1906 was caused by the San Andreas Fault?
58151.e: In 1906 the fault ruptured over a length of several hundred kilometres. The earthquake and fires destroyed large parts of San Francisco.
58151.m: The San Francisco earthquake of 1906 happened on the San Andreas Fault.

58152.q: Roughly how fast do the plates move against each other at the San Andreas Fault?
58152.e: The Pacific Plate moves relative to the North American Plate by around 3 to 5 cm per year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Because the plates lock together, the stress is released suddenly in earthquakes.
58152.m: At the San Andreas Fault, the plates move a few centimetres per year.

58153.q: What moves the sections of a mid-ocean ridge sideways against each other?
58153.e: Mid-ocean ridges are divided into many segments offset by transform faults. Only the part between the ridge ends is active; the extensions are called fracture zones.
58153.m: Transform faults divide the ocean ridges into sections.

58154.q: Which natural hazard is typical of transform faults?
58154.e: Because the plates lock and then suddenly let go, shallow, often strong earthquakes happen. There is usually no volcanism, because no melt forms.

58155.q: Which large transform fault runs across the north of Turkey?
58155.e: The North Anatolian Fault separates the Anatolian Plate from the Eurasian Plate. There have been repeated severe earthquakes along this fault, for example near Izmit in 1999.
58155.m: The North Anatolian Fault is a transform fault in Turkey.

58156.q: Which plates slide past each other at the transform fault through the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea?
58156.e: Here the Arabian Plate slides north past the African Plate. The Dead Sea lies in a basin along this fault.
58156.m: The Dead Sea lies on a transform fault between Arabia and Africa.

58157.q: Which two plates does the Mid-Atlantic Ridge separate in the North Atlantic?
58157.e: In the North Atlantic, the North American and Eurasian Plates are moving away from each other. On Iceland this plate boundary even comes up on land.
58157.m: In the North Atlantic, the ridge separates North America from Eurasia.

58158.q: Which island rose out of the sea from 1963 in an eruption south of Iceland?
58158.e: Surtsey formed from 1963 to 1967 in an undersea eruption in Iceland's volcanic zone. The island is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a laboratory for how living things settle new land.
58158.m: Surtsey is a young volcanic island off Iceland.

58159.q: Which island nation lies right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so that you can see the plate boundary on land there?
58159.e: Iceland lies over the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and also over a hotspot. That is why the ridge rises above sea level there, and the island gets about two centimetres wider every year.
58159.m: On Iceland, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge comes up on land.

58160.q: Which cartographer discovered the central valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in the 1950s?
58160.e: Marie Tharp analysed echo-sounding data with Bruce Heezen and recognised a continuous rift structure on the ridge. This was an important clue to sea-floor spreading.
58160.m: Marie Tharp discovered the central valley of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

58161.q: Which measuring method was used in the 20th century to recognise the Mid-Atlantic Ridge as a continuous mountain range on the sea floor?
58161.e: An echo sounder sends sound waves to the sea floor and measures the time until the echo comes back. Many measurements together showed a huge mountain range in the middle of the Atlantic.
58161.m: The sea floor was mapped with echo sounding.

58162.q: Where on Iceland can you dive in a fissure between the North American and Eurasian Plates?
a: Silfra fissure in Thingvellir National Park
58162.e: The Silfra fissure is filled with clear glacier water. It lies in the rift area of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which comes up on land on Iceland.
58162.m: In the Silfra fissure you dive between two continental plates.

58163.q: What happens at a mid-ocean ridge such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
a: Two plates move apart and new crust forms
One plate sinks beneath the other
Two plates collide and fold up mountains
Two plates slide sideways past each other
58163.e: At the ridge the plates move apart, magma rises and hardens into new sea floor. This is called a divergent plate boundary.
58163.m: New sea floor forms at mid-ocean ridges.

58164.q: Which supercontinent broke apart when the Atlantic began to open?
58164.e: Around 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to split between North America and Africa. Since then the Atlantic has been growing at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
58164.m: The Atlantic formed when Pangaea broke apart.

58165.q: Which rock makes up most of the crust that forms at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
58165.e: Basaltic magma forms from the rising mantle material. Oceanic crust therefore consists mainly of basalt and its deep-seated equivalent, gabbro.
58165.m: Oceanic crust consists mainly of basalt.

58166.q: Into which two sub-plates is the African Plate being split at the East African Rift?
58166.e: West of the rift lies the Nubian Plate, east of it the Somali Plate. The two are slowly moving away from each other.
58166.m: At the East African Rift, the Nubian and Somali Plates are separating.

58167.q: According to many geologists, what could the East African Rift become in many millions of years?
58167.e: If the stretching continues, the crust can tear apart completely and seawater can flow in. That is also how the Red Sea formed.
58167.m: A rift valley can become a new ocean.

58168.q: Which very deep lake lies in the western branch of the East African Rift?
58168.e: Lake Tanganyika is around 1,470 metres deep, making it the second-deepest lake on Earth. Lake Victoria, by contrast, lies in a shallow basin between the two branches of the rift.
58168.m: Lake Tanganyika fills a deep rift in East Africa.

58169.q: Why are there many volcanoes along the East African Rift?
a: The crust is stretched and thinner, and magma rises
An ocean plate sinks beneath Africa there
Meteorites have punched through the crust
58169.e: As the plates drift apart, the Earth's crust gets thinner, and magma from the mantle rises. This created volcanoes such as Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania, which produces a rare carbonate lava.
58169.m: Where the crust is torn apart, magma rises.

58170.q: What is the region in Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti called where the East African Rift, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden meet?
58170.e: In the Afar Triangle, three rift systems meet at a triple junction. Parts of the region lie below sea level, and it is very active volcanically.
58170.m: In the Afar Triangle, three rift systems meet.

58171.q: Which volcano in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is known for its lava lake?
58171.e: Nyiragongo lies in the western branch of the East African Rift near the city of Goma. Its very runny lava can flow away quickly, as in the eruptions of 1977, 2002 and 2021.
58171.m: Nyiragongo in the Congo has a lava lake.

58172.q: Which famous fossil of an early human relative was discovered in the Afar region in 1974?
58172.e: Lucy is a skeleton around 3.2 million years old of the species Australopithecus afarensis. In the rift, fossils are exposed by erosion of the rift shoulders.
58172.m: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in 1974.

58173.q: Which highest mountain in Africa is a volcano whose formation is linked to the East African Rift?
58173.e: Kilimanjaro is a stratovolcano around 5,895 metres high. The Rwenzori Mountains, by contrast, are an uplifted block of crust and not a volcano.
58173.m: Kilimanjaro is a volcano in East Africa.

58174.q: On average, how fast are the plates at the East African Rift moving away from each other?
a: Not at all, they are standing still
58174.e: On average, the plates drift apart by only a few millimetres per year. But sometimes it happens suddenly: in 2005 a crack around 60 km long opened up in the Afar region within days.
58174.m: Rifts usually open slowly, but sometimes suddenly.

58175.q: Roughly how many years ago did the Indian Plate begin to collide with Eurasia?
58175.e: The collision began in the Eocene around 50 million years ago. Since then India has been pushing north and lifting the Himalayas and Tibet.
58175.m: India has been pushing against Eurasia for around 50 million years.

58176.q: Which ocean closed as the Indian Plate moved north?
58176.e: In front of India lay the Tethys Ocean, whose floor sank beneath Eurasia. With the collision, this ocean between India and Asia disappeared.
58176.m: The Tethys disappeared between India and Asia.

58177.q: Which rocks form the summit of Mount Everest?
58177.e: The summit consists of limestone of the Qomolangma Formation, which was once deposited on the sea floor. The collision lifted it to almost 8,850 metres.
58177.m: The summit of Mount Everest was once sea floor.

58178.q: Why are there hardly any active volcanoes in the High Himalayas?
a: Two continental plates collide without deep subduction
The Himalayas lie on a hotspot
The crust there is especially thin
58178.e: Continental crust is too light to sink deep into the mantle. So hardly any magma forms, and instead the crust is stacked up and thickened.
58178.m: A continent-continent collision produces hardly any volcanoes.

58179.q: Roughly how thick is the Earth's crust beneath the Tibetan Plateau?
58179.e: The collision compressed and stacked up the crust. There it is about twice as thick as normal continental crust of around 35 kilometres.
58179.m: Beneath Tibet the Earth's crust is about twice as thick as normal.

58180.q: From which land mass did India finally separate around 90 million years ago?
58180.e: India first broke away from Africa together with Madagascar and separated from Madagascar in the Cretaceous. After that it moved quickly north.
58180.m: India separated from Madagascar in the Cretaceous.

58181.q: Which huge basalt layers formed around 66 million years ago when India moved over a hotspot?
58181.e: Enormous amounts of lava poured out above today's Réunion hotspot and formed the Deccan Traps. They cover large parts of western India.
58181.m: The Deccan Traps formed when India passed over a hotspot.

58182.q: Roughly how fast did India move north before the collision?
58182.e: Before the collision, India was one of the fastest plates known. After the collision it slowed to around 4 to 5 centimetres per year.
58182.m: Before the collision, India was an especially fast plate.

58183.q: Which severe earthquake of 2015 was a result of the collision of the Indian and Eurasian Plates?
