58624.q: Why is the seawater in the Humboldt Current off Peru colder than its position in the tropics would suggest?
a: Cold water from the south and rising deep water cool it.
Andean glaciers calve directly into the sea.
58624.e: The current brings water from higher southern latitudes, and in addition cold deep water rises off the coast. This means water temperatures off Lima are often well below 20 °C.
58624.m: The Humboldt Current is cold because its water comes from the south and from the depths.

58625.q: Which Köppen-Geiger climate group hardly occurs at all in the southern hemisphere outside mountains, because large land masses are missing at the right latitudes?
58625.e: D climates need large continents in middle to high latitudes, where severe cold develops in winter. In the southern hemisphere, there is almost only sea at these latitudes.
58625.m: Boreal D climates exist almost only in the northern hemisphere.

58626.q: Roughly what average surface temperature would the Earth have without the natural greenhouse effect?
58626.e: Without greenhouse gases, the Earth would hold only enough heat to reach about -18 °C. In fact the global average is about +15 °C, which is about 33 degrees higher.
58626.m: The natural greenhouse effect is what makes the Earth habitable.

58627.q: Since when has the warming effect of the atmosphere, today’s greenhouse effect, been described scientifically?
58627.e: As early as 1824, the Frenchman Joseph Fourier realised that the Earth would be much colder without an atmosphere. Later, researchers such as John Tyndall and Svante Arrhenius demonstrated the effect of CO2 and water vapour.
58627.m: The greenhouse effect has been known for almost 200 years.

58628.q: Which radiation do greenhouse gases mainly absorb?
58628.e: The Earth’s surface gives off energy as long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb this radiation and send some of it back to the Earth.
58628.m: Greenhouse gases hold back the Earth’s heat radiation.

58629.q: Why are nitrogen (N2) and oxygen (O2) not greenhouse gases, even though they make up most of the air?
a: They hardly absorb any heat radiation
They only occur at great heights
They dissolve straight away in seawater
They are heavier than carbon dioxide
58629.e: Greenhouse gases such as CO2 and water vapour absorb the Earth’s heat radiation. The simple molecules N2 and O2, on the other hand, let this radiation through almost unhindered.
58629.m: Only gases that absorb heat radiation act as greenhouse gases.

58630.q: Which Swedish chemist was the first to calculate, in 1896, how much a change in CO2 content changes the Earth’s temperature?
58630.e: In 1896 Svante Arrhenius estimated how the temperature changes with more or less CO2 in the air. He later received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, but for other work.
58630.m: In 1896 Svante Arrhenius laid the foundation for climate sensitivity.

58631.q: Which gases were shown in the laboratory in the 19th century to be important absorbers of heat radiation?
58631.e: From 1859 the physicist John Tyndall used an apparatus of his own to show that trace gases in particular, such as water vapour and CO2, strongly absorb heat radiation. The main gases of the air hardly do this.
58631.m: Water vapour and CO2 hold back heat radiation.

58632.q: Calculated over 100 years, how strong is the effect of methane compared with the same mass of CO2 (global warming potential)?
58632.e: The IPCC gives methane a global warming potential of about 28 to 30 over 100 years. Methane is very powerful but is broken down in the atmosphere after about twelve years.
58632.m: Methane is a short-lived but very powerful greenhouse gas.

58633.q: Which greenhouse gas contributes most to human-caused warming worldwide?
58633.e: Per kilogram, methane, nitrous oxide or sulphur hexafluoride are more powerful. But because huge amounts of CO2 are released from coal, oil and natural gas, CO2 causes most of the warming.
58633.m: Because of its large quantity, CO2 is the most important human-made greenhouse gas.

58634.q: For every degree of warming, the air can hold about 7 per cent more water vapour. What is the resulting amplification called?
58634.e: Warmer air holds more water vapour, and this water vapour strengthens the greenhouse effect further. This positive feedback roughly doubles the warming caused by CO2 alone.
58634.m: Water vapour feedback amplifies any warming.

58635.q: On which volcano is the famous series of measurements known as the Keeling Curve recorded?
a: Mount St. Helens in the USA
58635.e: The measuring station is at about 3400 m on Mauna Loa, far away from large sources of emissions. The air there is well mixed and representative of the northern hemisphere.
58635.m: The Keeling Curve comes from Mauna Loa in Hawaii.

58636.q: In which year did the continuous CO2 measurements of the Keeling Curve begin?
58636.e: Charles David Keeling started the measurements in 1958. Since then it has been the longest unbroken series of direct measurements of the CO2 content of the air.
58636.m: The Keeling Curve has run without a break since 1958.

58637.q: Why does the Keeling Curve show a regular rise and fall every year?
a: Plants in the northern hemisphere grow and decay
Heating is used in winter in the southern hemisphere
The volcanoes in Hawaii are only active in certain seasons
Solar activity varies over the year
58637.e: In the northern hemisphere’s summer, the many plants there take up CO2, and in autumn and winter it is released again as they decompose. Because the northern hemisphere has much more land, it shapes the curve.
58637.m: The yearly zigzags of the Keeling Curve are the breathing of the plant world.

58638.q: In which month does the CO2 content at Mauna Loa reach its highest value each year?
58638.e: Until spring, decomposition outweighs growth, so the CO2 content rises until about May. After that, the growing plants take up a lot of CO2 and the value falls until autumn.
58638.m: At Mauna Loa, CO2 reaches its peak every year in May.

58639.q: Roughly what CO2 content did Keeling measure at the start of his series of measurements?
58639.e: The first measurements in 1958 gave about 315 ppm. Today the value is well above 420 ppm.
58639.m: Since the Keeling measurements began, the CO2 content has risen by more than 100 ppm.

58640.q: In which year was the daily average at Mauna Loa above 400 ppm CO2 for the first time?
58640.e: In May 2013 a daily average above 400 ppm was measured at Mauna Loa for the first time. A few years later the annual average was also permanently above that.
58640.m: Since 2013 the CO2 content has at times been above 400 ppm.

58641.q: By how much did the CO2 content at Mauna Loa rise in the calendar year 2024, the largest rise since measurements began?
58641.e: Over the course of 2024 the value rose by about 3.6 ppm, more than ever before in a calendar year of the series (as of 2025). The reasons were high fossil fuel emissions as well as wildfires and El Niño.
58641.m: 2024 brought the largest CO2 rise in the Keeling Curve so far.

58642.q: A CO2 content of 420 ppm corresponds to what share of the volume of air?
58642.e: ppm means “parts per million”, in other words millionths. 420 millionths are 420 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.00042, which is 0.042 per cent.
58642.m: One ppm is a millionth, in other words a ten-thousandth of a per cent.

58643.q: Which US researcher started the CO2 measurements at Mauna Loa?
58643.e: The chemist Charles David Keeling from the Scripps Institution in California started the measurements. After his death in 2005, his son Ralph Keeling continued the work.
58643.m: The Keeling Curve bears the name of its founder, Charles David Keeling.

58644.q: In which year was the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) founded?
58644.e: The IPCC was set up in 1988. Its First Assessment Report appeared in 1990.

58645.q: Which two UN organisations founded the IPCC?
58645.e: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) founded the IPCC together. The UN General Assembly confirmed its founding.
58645.m: The IPCC was created by the WMO and UNEP.

58646.q: In which city is the secretariat of the IPCC based?
58646.e: The IPCC secretariat is based at the World Meteorological Organization in Geneva. Bonn, on the other hand, is home to the secretariat of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
58646.m: The IPCC has its secretariat in Geneva.

58647.q: Which organisation received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007 together with Al Gore for its work on climate change?
58647.e: The IPCC and the former US Vice President Al Gore were honoured in 2007. They had spread knowledge about human-made climate change.
58647.m: The IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007.

58648.q: How are the IPCC’s assessment reports produced?
a: The IPCC runs its own measuring stations
A UN computing centre creates new models
58648.e: The IPCC does not do research itself. Hundreds of scientists summarise and assess the state of the published scientific literature.
58648.m: The IPCC summarises existing research instead of doing research itself.

58649.q: What happens to the “Summary for Policymakers” of an IPCC report before it is published?
a: Governments approve it line by line
A court checks it for accuracy
It is kept secret until the next COP
It is written by a single person
58649.e: The delegates of the member states approve the summary sentence by sentence together with the authors. Its content must match the scientific report.
58649.m: The summary of an IPCC report is approved jointly by all governments.

58650.q: What do ice cores from Antarctica show, which researchers at the University of Bern also analyse for the IPCC reports?
a: What the air was made of in earlier times
How old the Earth is altogether
Where volcanoes used to be in Europe
How much oil lies beneath the ice
58650.e: Tiny bubbles of air are trapped in the ice. From them, the CO2 content of the atmosphere can be determined over hundreds of thousands of years. Bern is a centre of this research.
58650.m: Ice cores are an archive of the air of past times.

58651.q: According to the Sixth Assessment Report, how much warmer was the global surface temperature in 2011 to 2020 than in 1850 to 1900?
58651.e: The Sixth Assessment Report gives a warming of about 1.1 °C for the decade 2011 to 2020 compared with 1850 to 1900. It describes the human influence as unequivocal.
58651.m: In the decade up to 2020, the Earth was about 1.1 degrees warmer than before industrialisation.

58652.q: Why does the IPCC use fixed terms such as “likely” or “very likely” in its reports?
a: To express how certain a statement is in a consistent way
To make the reports easier to read
To hide errors in the measurements
Because numbers are banned in UN reports
58652.e: Each term stands for a fixed range of probability, “very likely”, for example, for 90 to 100 per cent. This means the words mean the same thing in every chapter.
58652.m: The IPCC expresses uncertainty with fixed terms.

58653.q: Which long-term climate target did Swiss voters approve in 2023 with the Climate and Innovation Act?
58653.e: In June 2023 the people approved the law. By 2050 Switzerland should no longer emit more greenhouse gases than are stored naturally or technically.
58653.m: Switzerland wants to be climate-neutral by 2050.

58654.q: In which year did the Paris Agreement come into force?
58654.e: The agreement came into force on 4 November 2016, less than a year after it was adopted. That was unusually fast for a UN treaty.
58654.m: The Paris Agreement has applied since November 2016.

58655.q: Why did the Paris Agreement not come into force as soon as it was adopted in 2015?
a: Enough countries first had to ratify it
The UN General Assembly first rejected it
The USA first had to sign it
It first had to be translated into all languages
58655.e: At least 55 countries accounting for 55 per cent of emissions had to ratify it. This threshold was reached in October 2016.
58655.m: An agreement only applies once enough countries have ratified it.

58656.q: What are the national climate targets that each country submits under the Paris Agreement called?
58656.e: The countries set their contributions themselves, the so-called NDCs. These nationally determined contributions are the heart of the agreement.
58656.m: Under the Paris Agreement, each country sets its own climate targets.

58657.q: How often do countries have to present new climate targets under the Paris Agreement?
58657.e: Every five years, each country has to submit a new target that is as ambitious as possible. This is called the ambition mechanism.
58657.m: The Paris climate targets are tightened every five years.

58658.q: Before the Paris Agreement, which treaty from 1997 committed only industrialised countries to binding emission targets?
58658.e: In the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, only industrialised countries had fixed reduction targets. The Paris Agreement, by contrast, includes all countries.
58658.m: The Kyoto Protocol was the forerunner of the Paris Agreement.

58659.q: In which city was the first Global Stocktake of the Paris Agreement completed in 2023?
58659.e: The first Global Stocktake was completed at COP28 in Dubai. It found that the world is not on track and called for a transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.
58659.m: At COP28 in Dubai, the world officially took stock of the Paris Agreement for the first time.

58660.q: According to its Paris climate target, by how much does Switzerland want to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 1990?
58660.e: Switzerland has committed to halving its emissions by 2030 compared with 1990. Part of this may be achieved through projects abroad.
58660.m: Switzerland wants to halve its emissions by 2030 compared with 1990.

58661.q: What does Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allow Switzerland to do?
a: Count climate protection abroad towards its own target
Emit more CO2 than other countries
58661.e: Switzerland funds projects, for example in Peru or Ghana, and counts the emissions saved towards its target. It signed the first such agreement with Peru in 2020.
58661.m: Through Article 6, Switzerland counts climate projects abroad.

58662.q: In which year did the IPCC publish its special report on global warming of 1.5 °C?
58662.e: The Paris climate conference had asked the IPCC for this report. It appeared in October 2018 and showed the large differences between 1.5 and 2 degrees.
58662.m: The IPCC special report on the 1.5-degree target appeared in 2018.

58663.q: According to the IPCC special report, by how much would global CO2 emissions have to fall by 2030 compared with 2010 to reach 1.5 °C?
58663.e: In the pathways with no or only a small overshoot, CO2 emissions fall by about 45 per cent by 2030 compared with 2010. After that they have to keep falling to zero.
58663.m: For 1.5 degrees, CO2 emissions would have to almost halve by 2030.

58664.q: According to the IPCC special report, around when do global CO2 emissions have to reach net zero to limit warming to 1.5 °C?
58664.e: The 1.5-degree pathways reach net zero CO2 around the middle of the century. For 2 degrees, this point is only reached around 2070.
58664.m: The 1.5-degree target requires net zero CO2 by the middle of the century.

58665.q: According to the IPCC, 70 to 90 per cent of warm-water coral reefs decline at 1.5 °C. How many is it at 2 °C?
58665.e: According to the IPCC special report, practically all warm-water coral reefs would disappear at 2 °C. This shows how much difference half a degree makes.
58665.m: Every tenth of a degree counts, especially for coral reefs.

58666.q: According to the IPCC, how often can an ice-free Arctic summer be expected with 2 °C of global warming?
58666.e: At 1.5 °C, an ice-free Arctic summer can be expected about once a century; at 2 °C, about once a decade.
58666.m: Half a degree more makes ice-free summers in the Arctic ten times more frequent.

58667.q: Which calendar year was the first in which the global average temperature was more than 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial level?
58667.e: According to the WMO and Copernicus, 2024 was the first calendar year above the 1.5 °C mark (as of 2025). 2023 was just below it.
58667.m: 2024 was the first calendar year above 1.5 degrees of warming.

58668.q: Why is the 1.5-degree target not considered missed as soon as a single year is above 1.5 °C?
a: It refers to an average over about 20 years
It only applies from the year 2100
It only concerns the sea temperature
It only measures the temperature in Europe
58668.e: The target refers to long-term warming, which is determined as an average over about two decades. Individual years vary, for example because of El Niño.
58668.m: The 1.5-degree target refers to a long-term average, not to a single year.

58669.q: At the start of 2024, the remaining CO2 budget for 1.5 °C was estimated at about 200 Gt CO2. How long will it last at about 40 Gt a year?
58669.e: 200 Gt ÷ 40 Gt per year = 5 years. The budget applies to a 50 per cent chance of not exceeding 1.5 °C.
58669.m: If emissions stay the same, the 1.5-degree budget will be used up in a few years.

58670.q: Which group of countries campaigned particularly strongly for the 1.5-degree target in the negotiations?
a: The Alliance of Small Island States
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
58670.e: The small island states (AOSIS) are particularly threatened by rising sea levels. Their motto was “1.5 to stay alive”.
58670.m: The small island states fought hardest for the 1.5-degree target.

58671.q: According to the IPCC, by how much did the global mean sea level rise from 1901 to 2018?
58671.e: The IPCC gives a rise of about 0.20 m for this period. The rise has clearly speeded up in recent decades.
58671.m: Since 1900 the sea level has risen by about 20 centimetres.

58672.q: Besides the melting of glaciers and ice sheets, which process contributes most to sea level rise?
58672.e: Water expands when it warms up. Because the oceans take up over 90 per cent of the extra heat, the sea level rises noticeably from this alone.
58672.m: Warm seawater takes up more space and makes the sea level rise.

58673.q: Why does melting sea ice hardly make the sea level rise at all?
a: Floating ice already displaces its own weight in water
Sea ice evaporates directly into the air
Sea ice is made of fresh water and sinks
58673.e: According to Archimedes’ principle, floating ice displaces exactly as much water as it weighs. When it melts, it fills this space; only ice on land raises the sea level.
58673.m: Only land ice makes the sea level rise when it melts.

58674.q: Why is the relative sea level falling on some coasts of Scandinavia despite the global rise?
a: The land has been rising since the Ice Age
The Baltic Sea evaporates particularly strongly
The tides are particularly weak there
58674.e: After the Ice Age ice sheet melted, the Earth’s crust, freed of its load, is still rising today, by almost a centimetre a year in the Gulf of Bothnia. That is more than the global sea level rise.
58674.m: Where the land is rising, the sea level can seem to fall.

58675.q: How much sea level rise is stored in the entire Antarctic ice sheet?
58675.e: The Antarctic ice sheet is the largest store of ice on Earth. Its ice corresponds to a sea level equivalent of about 58 m.
58675.m: Most of the Earth’s ice lies in Antarctica.

58676.q: With which method has global sea level been measured from space since 1993?
58676.e: Satellites such as TOPEX/Poseidon and their successors use radar to measure the distance to the sea surface. This creates an almost global series of measurements.
58676.m: Satellites measure the height of the seas with radar.

58677.q: According to the IPCC, how fast did the global sea level rise on average between 2006 and 2018?
58677.e: The IPCC gives about 3.7 mm per year for 2006 to 2018. At the beginning of the 20th century, it was only about 1.3 mm per year.
58677.m: Today the sea level is rising almost three times as fast as a hundred years ago.

58678.q: Which island state signed a treaty with Australia in 2023 that allows its citizens to move there because of rising sea levels?
58678.e: Under the Falepili Union, up to 280 people from Tuvalu each year receive the right to live in Australia. The highest points of Tuvalu are only a few metres above the sea.
58678.m: Because of the rising sea, Tuvalu is seeking protection from Australia.

58679.q: According to the IPCC, how much is global sea level likely to rise by 2100 with very high emissions (SSP5-8.5)?
58679.e: The Sixth Assessment Report gives a likely range of 0.63 to 1.01 m compared with 1995 to 2014 for this scenario. A higher rise cannot be ruled out if ice sheets become unstable.
58679.m: With high emissions, the sea level could rise by almost a metre by 2100.

58680.q: Which disease broke out on the Yamal Peninsula in 2016 after thawing permafrost had exposed an old animal carcass?
58680.e: During a heatwave, a reindeer carcass infected with anthrax thawed out. The spores had survived in the frozen ground and caused an outbreak among reindeer and people.
58680.m: Thawing permafrost can release old pathogens.

58681.q: According to the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), roughly how much of Switzerland’s land area lies in permafrost?
58681.e: Model calculations show that about 5 per cent of Switzerland’s land area is affected by permafrost. That is more than the area of all Swiss glaciers.
58681.m: In Switzerland, permafrost lies under about a twentieth of the land.

58682.q: What share of the land area of the northern hemisphere has permafrost beneath it?
58682.e: About 24 per cent of the land area of the northern hemisphere lies above permafrost, mainly in Siberia, Canada, Alaska and on the Tibetan Plateau.
58682.m: A quarter of the land in the northern hemisphere is permanently frozen.

58683.q: How much carbon do the northern permafrost soils store compared with today’s atmosphere?
a: About a hundred times as much
58683.e: An estimated 1400 to 1600 Gt of carbon are stored in permafrost soils, about twice as much as in the atmosphere. If the ground thaws, microbes can turn it into CO2 and methane.
58683.m: Twice as much carbon lies dormant in permafrost as in the air.

58684.q: What are tongue-shaped masses of rock debris with ice inside, which creep slowly downhill in high mountains, called?
58684.e: Rock glaciers consist of rock debris and ice and are a visible sign of permafrost. In the Swiss Alps, many of them are now creeping much faster than in the past.
58684.m: Rock glaciers indicate permafrost in the mountains.

58685.q: What are the hollows and lakes called that form when ice-rich permafrost thaws and the ground sinks?
58685.e: In thermokarst, the ground ice melts and the surface sinks unevenly. Hollows, ponds and lakes form, which speed up the thawing further.
58685.m: Thermokarst forms when ice-rich ground thaws and sinks.

58686.q: Which huge collapse crater in Yakutia is a symbol of thawing permafrost?
58686.e: The Batagaika crater in north-eastern Siberia has been growing for decades because the permafrost at its edges is thawing and breaking off. It is more than a kilometre long.
58686.m: The Batagaika crater shows impressively how thawing permafrost changes the landscape.

58687.q: What is the Swiss monitoring network that observes changes in permafrost in the Alps called?
58687.e: PERMOS stands for Permafrost Monitoring Switzerland and measures, among other things, temperatures in boreholes. GLAMOS, by contrast, monitors glaciers, and NABEL air quality.
58687.m: The PERMOS network monitors permafrost in the Swiss Alps.

58688.q: Why do mountain villages such as Pontresina build protective embankments when the permafrost above them thaws?
a: The thawing ground loses its hold and debris flows threaten
The meltwater immediately floods the whole valley
The ground becomes red-hot when it thaws
58688.e: Ice in the ground acts like glue for debris and rock. When it thaws, slopes become unstable. That is why Pontresina built large embankments in 2003 against debris flows and avalanches from the Schafberg.
58688.m: Pontresina protects itself with embankments from the effects of thawing permafrost.

58689.q: What is meant by a tipping point in the climate system?
a: A threshold beyond which a system changes into a new state in a self-reinforcing way
The day with the highest temperature of a year
The boundary between two climate zones
The moment from which greenhouse gases break down by themselves
58689.e: Once a tipping point is passed, an ice sheet or a rainforest, for example, keeps changing even without any further push. The concept of tipping elements became well known in 2008 through Timothy Lenton and his team.
58689.m: After a tipping point, part of the climate system keeps changing by itself.

58690.q: Which type of feedback drives a tipping element into a new state after the tipping point is passed?
58690.e: After the tipping point, the change reinforces itself, even without any further push. Negative feedbacks, by contrast, would stabilise the system.
58690.m: Self-reinforcing feedbacks turn small changes into big upheavals.

58691.q: What would a collapse of the Atlantic overturning circulation mean for north-western Europe?
58691.e: The circulation brings a lot of heat into the North Atlantic. Without it, north-western Europe would become much colder despite global warming.
58691.m: Without the Atlantic overturning circulation, north-western Europe would cool down.

58692.q: What threatens the Amazon rainforest if it passes its tipping point?
a: It grows faster towards the Andes
58692.e: Deforestation and droughts reduce the evaporation that produces the rain in the Amazon region itself. If too little rain falls, large areas of the forest could turn into dry savanna.
58692.m: An Amazon rainforest that has tipped could become savanna.

58693.q: Which feedback speeds up the melting of sea ice because dark water absorbs more sunlight than bright ice?
58693.e: Ice reflects most of the sunlight, while the dark sea absorbs a lot of it. Less ice means more warming and therefore even less ice.
58693.m: Shrinking ice makes the Earth absorb even more of the sun’s heat.

58694.q: What is it called when a system that has tipped only returns to its old state at a much lower temperature than the one at which it tipped?
58694.e: With hysteresis, the state of a system depends on its history. That is why a melted ice sheet does not simply rebuild itself when the temperature falls back to the old value.
58694.m: Because of hysteresis, tipping elements that have tipped can hardly be brought back.

58695.q: Why is the West Antarctic Ice Sheet considered particularly unstable?
a: It rests on bedrock below sea level
It lies directly on active volcanoes
It consists mainly of sea ice
58695.e: Much of the ice sheet rests on bedrock that lies below sea level and gets deeper further inland. Warm seawater can therefore push under the ice and trigger a self-reinforcing retreat.
58695.m: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet is vulnerable because warm seawater can reach under it.

58696.q: Which glacier in West Antarctica is often called the “Doomsday Glacier” because of the risk it poses?
58696.e: The Thwaites Glacier is about the size of Great Britain and acts like a cork holding back other masses of ice. Its break-up could destabilise West Antarctica and raise sea levels by several metres in the long term.
58696.m: The Thwaites Glacier is key to the stability of West Antarctica.

58697.q: According to the 2025 “Global Tipping Points Report”, which tipping element has already passed its tipping point?
58697.e: In 2025 the report found that warm-water coral reefs have passed their thermal tipping point. Repeated marine heatwaves are causing coral bleaching over large areas.
58697.m: Coral reefs are considered the first tipping element that has already tipped.

58698.q: Roughly what share of the CO2 emitted by humans have the oceans taken up?
58698.e: The seas have taken up about a quarter of human-made CO2 emissions. This slows down warming but changes the chemistry of seawater.
58698.m: The sea swallows about a quarter of our CO2 and becomes more acidic as a result.

58699.q: How has the average pH of ocean surface water changed since industrialisation?
58699.e: The pH has fallen by about 0.1 units. The sea is still slightly alkaline but is becoming more acidic.
58699.m: Seawater is slightly alkaline, but its pH is falling.

58700.q: By what percentage does the concentration of hydrogen ions rise when the pH falls by 0.1?
58700.e: The pH scale is logarithmic: the concentration changes by a factor of 10 to the power of 0.1, which is about 1.26. That means about 26 per cent more hydrogen ions.
58700.m: Even a small change in pH means a lot more acid.

58701.q: Which acid forms when CO2 dissolves in seawater?
58701.e: CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid (H2CO3). This releases hydrogen ions, which lowers the pH.
58701.m: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid in the sea.

58702.q: Why do mussels, corals and sea urchins suffer particularly from ocean acidification?
a: Fewer carbonate ions are available for limestone shells
The water suddenly contains no more oxygen
The salt in the sea crystallises out
58702.e: The extra hydrogen ions bind carbonate ions. Creatures that build limestone then need more energy to build their shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate.
58702.m: More acidic seawater makes it harder to build limestone shells.

58703.q: Which particularly soluble form of calcium carbonate do corals and sea butterflies form?
58703.e: Aragonite dissolves more easily than calcite. Creatures with aragonite shells are therefore particularly sensitive to more acidic water.
58703.m: Aragonite is the most sensitive form of limestone in the sea.

58704.q: By which catchphrase is ocean acidification often mentioned alongside global warming?
58704.e: Ocean acidification has the same cause as warming, namely CO2, but acts chemically rather than through temperature. That is why it is called “the other CO2 problem”.
58704.m: Ocean acidification is the second big problem caused by CO2.

58705.q: What does it mean when researchers classify ocean acidification as a planetary boundary that has been crossed?
a: The risk of large changes that are hard to reverse increases
Not a single animal lives in the sea any more
Seawater is as acidic as vinegar
The seas no longer take up any CO2
58705.e: The planetary boundaries describe a safe operating space for humanity. In 2025 ocean acidification was classified as the seventh of nine boundaries to have been crossed.
58705.m: With ocean acidification, another planetary boundary has been crossed.

58706.q: Why are the seas in the polar regions becoming acidic particularly quickly?
a: There are more underwater volcanoes there
No plants live in the sea there
58706.e: Gases dissolve better in cold water than in warm water. That is why polar seas take up a lot of CO2, and aragonite becomes scarce there first.
58706.m: Cold seas take up more CO2 and become acidic faster.

58707.q: What does “net zero” mean for greenhouse gas emissions?
a: Remaining emissions are balanced by removals
No greenhouse gas at all is emitted any more
Only industrialised countries still emit greenhouse gases
58707.e: With net zero, no more greenhouse gas is emitted than is permanently removed from the atmosphere again. Remaining emissions that are hard to avoid, for example from farming, must therefore be balanced out.
58707.m: Net zero means that emissions and removals balance each other out.

58708.q: By which year does Switzerland want to reach net zero under the Climate and Innovation Act?
58708.e: The Climate and Innovation Act states that Switzerland will emit no net greenhouse gases by 2050. It also contains interim targets for buildings, transport and industry.
58708.m: Switzerland wants to become climate-neutral by 2050.

58709.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the Climate and Innovation Act on 18 June 2023?
58709.e: The law was approved with 59.1 per cent voting yes. Two years earlier, the revised CO2 Act had narrowly failed.
58709.m: The Climate and Innovation Act was clearly approved in 2023.

58710.q: Which popular initiative was conditionally withdrawn in favour of the Climate and Innovation Act?
58710.e: The Glacier Initiative called for a ban on fossil fuels from 2050. After the yes vote on the counter-proposal, the withdrawal became final.
58710.m: The Climate and Innovation Act is the counter-proposal to the Glacier Initiative.

58711.q: Which proposal did Swiss voters narrowly reject on 13 June 2021?
58711.e: The revised CO2 Act was rejected with 51.6 per cent voting no. Among other things, it included a levy on plane tickets.
58711.m: The revised CO2 Act failed at the ballot box in 2021.

58712.q: What does the abbreviation DACCS stand for?
a: Capturing CO2 directly from the air and storing it
Decentralised use of waste heat in cities
58712.e: DACCS stands for Direct Air Carbon Capture and Storage. Plants suck in air, filter out the CO2 and store it permanently underground.
58712.m: DACCS takes CO2 directly from the air and stores it.

58713.q: What does the abbreviation BECCS stand for?
a: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage
58713.e: In BECCS, biomass is burned to produce energy, and the resulting CO2 is captured and stored. Because the plants took up CO2 beforehand, this creates negative emissions.
58713.m: BECCS combines bioenergy with storing CO2.

58714.q: In the Carbfix process in Iceland, in which rock is CO2 mineralised into solid carbonate?
58714.e: The CO2 is dissolved in water and pumped into the basalt. With calcium, magnesium and iron from the rock, it forms carbonate minerals within a few years.
58714.m: Basalt can turn CO2 into stone.

58715.q: By when does China want to reach carbon neutrality?
58715.e: In 2020 China announced that it would become carbon-neutral before 2060. Germany aims to do so by 2045, India by 2070.
58715.m: China is aiming for carbon neutrality by 2060.

58716.q: Roughly how much CO2 from fossil sources did one person cause per year on global average around 2023?
58716.e: The Global Carbon Project gives about 4.7 tonnes of CO2 per person for 2023. The figures vary greatly between countries.
58716.m: Worldwide, each person emits on average about five tonnes of CO2 a year.

58717.q: Where does the larger part of the Swiss population’s greenhouse gas footprint arise?
58717.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, more than half of the emissions from Swiss consumption arise abroad, for example in the production of imported goods. The domestic inventory does not show these emissions.
58717.m: Swiss consumption causes many emissions abroad.

58718.q: Which oil company made the idea of a personal carbon footprint well known with a campaign in the mid-2000s?
58718.e: Around 2004 BP introduced an online calculator for personal carbon footprints. Critics see this as an attempt to shift responsibility onto individuals.
58718.m: The idea of a personal carbon footprint was made popular by an oil company.

58719.q: Which Swiss person developed the concept of the ecological footprint together with William Rees?
58719.e: Mathis Wackernagel developed the concept in the 1990s at the University of British Columbia. The carbon footprint is part of it.
58719.m: The ecological footprint comes from the Swiss Mathis Wackernagel and William Rees.

58720.q: In which unit is the effect of different greenhouse gases combined in a carbon footprint?
58720.e: Each gas is converted, using its global warming potential, into the amount of CO2 that would have the same effect. This means methane, nitrous oxide and CO2 can be added together.
58720.m: CO2 equivalents make different greenhouse gases comparable.

58721.q: What are the emissions called that arise from making, transporting and disposing of a building or product?
58721.e: Embodied emissions are hidden in a product because they arise before or after it is used. In new buildings they often make up a large part of the total emissions.
58721.m: Embodied emissions are hidden in every product.

58722.q: Which part of the Greenhouse Gas Protocol covers emissions in the supply chain and from the use of products sold?
58722.e: Scope 1 covers a company’s direct emissions, Scope 2 those from purchased energy. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions and is often the largest part.
58722.m: Scope 3 covers the emissions of the whole value chain.

58723.q: A car emits 150 g of CO2 per kilometre and drives 12,000 km a year. How much CO2 does this produce?
58723.e: 150 g × 12,000 = 1,800,000 g. That is 1800 kg, or 1.8 tonnes of CO2.
58723.m: Kilometres driven times emissions per kilometre gives the amount of CO2.

58724.q: Which of these foods usually has the largest carbon footprint per kilogram?
58724.e: Cattle release a lot of methane during digestion and need a lot of feed and land. That is why beef causes many times the emissions of chicken or plant foods per kilogram.
58724.m: Beef is one of the foods that harms the climate most.

58725.q: Roughly how high is the closed canopy of the tropical rainforest?
58725.e: The canopy forms an almost closed roof of leaves. Only individual, even taller trees stick out above it.
58725.m: The rainforest canopy is about 30 to 40 metres high.

58726.q: Roughly what share of sunlight reaches the forest floor in the tropical rainforest?
58726.e: The dense canopy and the layers beneath it catch almost all the light. It is therefore dim on the ground, and only shade-tolerant plants thrive.
58726.m: Only a tiny part of the light reaches the floor of the rainforest.

58727.q: What is the function of the buttress roots of many rainforest trees?
a: They store rainwater for the dry season.
They protect the trunk from fire.
58727.e: The soils are poor in nutrients, so the roots stay close to the surface. The broad, board-like root growths still give the tall trees stability.
58727.m: Buttress roots give tall, shallow-rooted trees support.

58728.q: What is the plant called that often germinates high up in a tree, sends aerial roots down to the ground and eventually encloses its host tree?
58728.e: The strangler fig begins its life in the light of the canopy. Its roots grow around the trunk of the host, which often dies and leaves behind a hollow fig trunk.
58728.m: The strangler fig grows from the top down and encloses its host.

58729.q: What is the job of the drip tips on the leaves of many rainforest plants?
a: They store water in the leaf.
58729.e: Water flows quickly off the leaf through the long, drawn-out tip. This means the leaf dries faster and is less colonised by algae, fungi and lichens.
58729.m: Drip tips let rainwater drip quickly off the leaf.

58730.q: How many species of tree can be found on a single hectare of the Amazon rainforest?
58730.e: In studies in the western Amazon region, well over 200 tree species were counted on one hectare. In a Swiss forest there are usually only a few species.
58730.m: The rainforest is extremely rich in species, even in the smallest area.

58731.q: Why do young trees in the rainforest grow particularly quickly when a forest giant falls?
a: A lot of light suddenly falls on the ground through the gap.
The fallen trunk immediately releases a lot of water.
The fall digs up the ground deeply.
The temperature on the ground drops sharply.
58731.e: Many young trees on the dark forest floor are waiting for more light. In a gap they grow up quickly until the canopy closes again.
58731.m: Gaps that let in light make young growth in the rainforest shoot upwards.

58732.q: Why do many plants in the herb layer of the rainforest have particularly large leaves?
a: This lets them catch as much of the scarce light as possible.
This lets them store water for the dry season.
This protects the ground from frost.
58732.e: Hardly any light reaches the ground. Large, thin leaves increase the area for photosynthesis.
58732.m: Large leaves help plants on the dark forest floor.

58733.q: What are woody climbing plants called that root in the ground and grow up trees into the canopy?
58733.e: Lianas save themselves the effort of a strong trunk of their own and use trees as support to reach the light. They often connect several tree crowns.
58733.m: Lianas climb up trees towards the light.

58734.q: According to the usual classification, roughly how many humid months does a wet savanna have?
58734.e: The further you go from the equator, the fewer wet months there are. The wet savanna has about 7 to 9.5, the dry savanna about 4.5 to 7 and the thorn savanna about 2 to 4.5 humid months.
58734.m: The more wet months, the lusher the savanna.

58735.q: Which type of savanna borders the desert and has only about 2 to 4.5 humid months?
58735.e: The thorn savanna is the driest type of savanna, with sparse grass and thorny shrubs such as acacias. It leads into semi-desert and desert.
58735.m: The thorn savanna is the driest form of savanna.

58736.q: What causes the rainy season in the savannas?
a: The Intertropical Convergence Zone moves with the overhead sun.
Cold ocean currents bring moist air.
Westerly winds bring low-pressure areas from the sea.
Mountains hold back moist trade winds all year.
58736.e: When the sun is directly overhead, the Intertropical Convergence Zone with its thundery rain moves into the area. That is why it is called zenithal rain.
58736.m: The savanna’s rainy season follows the overhead sun.

58737.q: What are the narrow strips of forest that grow along rivers in the savanna called?
58737.e: By the river, the trees have enough water even in the dry season. This creates a narrow fringe of forest in the middle of the grassland.
58737.m: Gallery forests line the rivers in the savanna.

58738.q: What is the vast savanna region in Venezuela and Colombia, drained by the Orinoco, called?
58738.e: The Llanos are wide tropical grasslands that are flooded over large areas in the rainy season. They are used mainly for cattle farming.
58738.m: The Llanos are the savannas of the Orinoco.

58739.q: What is the large savanna region in Brazil with tree savannas, much of which is now being converted for soya growing, called?
58739.e: The Cerrado covers large parts of central Brazil and is considered the most species-rich savanna in the world. A large part of it has already been turned into farmland and pasture.
58739.m: The Cerrado is Brazil’s great savanna.

58740.q: Which national park in Tanzania is known for the yearly migration of over a million wildebeest?
58740.e: In a yearly cycle, the wildebeest follow the rain and the fresh grass between the Serengeti and the Masai Mara in Kenya. It is one of the largest animal migrations on Earth.
58740.m: Huge herds of wildebeest migrate through the Serengeti every year.

58741.q: What role do natural fires play in the savanna?
a: They prevent a closed forest from forming.
They turn the savanna into desert for good.
58741.e: After a fire, grasses quickly sprout again from their protected buds, whereas young trees are often damaged. This keeps the grassland open.

58742.q: Which area south of the Sahara forms the transition from thorn savanna to desert?
58742.e: The word Sahel comes from Arabic and means the “shore” of the desert. The Sahel is strongly affected by changing rainfall and droughts.
58742.m: The Sahel is the fringe on the southern edge of the Sahara.

58743.q: What is another technical name for the taiga?
58743.e: The taiga stretches as a broad belt across North America, Scandinavia and Russia. The word “boreal” means “northern”.
58743.m: The taiga is the boreal coniferous forest of the north.

58744.q: Why is there practically no taiga in the southern hemisphere?
a: There is hardly any land at the right latitudes there.
It is too dry there at these latitudes.
The right tree species are missing there because of logging.
This zone lies under the Antarctic ice sheet there.
58744.e: Between about 50 and 70 degrees south there is almost nothing but ocean. That is why the taiga is a landscape zone of the northern hemisphere.
58744.m: The taiga exists almost only in the northern hemisphere.

58745.q: Which tree dominates the taiga in eastern Siberia and sheds its needles in autumn?
58745.e: The larch is a deciduous conifer. By shedding its needles, it survives the extremely cold and dry winters of eastern Siberia better than evergreen species.
58745.m: The larch is the only common conifer that loses its needles in winter.

58746.q: Which type of soil is typical of the taiga?
58746.e: The acidic needle litter breaks down only slowly. Acids wash iron and aluminium out of the topsoil, creating a pale bleached layer.
58746.m: The typical soil of the taiga is the bleached podzol.

58747.q: What advantage do evergreen conifers have in the taiga?
a: They can start photosynthesis straight away in spring.
They take up more water in winter.
They grow faster than broadleaf trees.
They form a particularly nutrient-rich soil.
58747.e: Because the needles do not have to be grown again every year, the trees can make full use of the short growing season. The small, wax-coated needles also lose little water.
58747.m: Evergreen needles make use of the short growing season straight away.

58748.q: Roughly how long is the growing season in the taiga?
58748.e: The winters are long and very cold, the summers short but relatively warm. The trees can only grow during this short time.
58748.m: The taiga has a short growing season of a few months.

58749.q: Which language does the word “taiga” come from?
58749.e: The word was taken into other languages through Russian and refers to the vast coniferous forests of Siberia. It probably goes back to a Turkic-Mongolian root.
58749.m: The word taiga reached us through Russian.

58750.q: What climate is found in the interior of the Siberian taiga?
a: extremely continental climate with large yearly variations
58750.e: Far from the sea, temperatures vary greatly between very cold winters and warm summers. In places such as Oymyakon, temperatures below minus 60 °C have been measured.
58750.m: In the interior of Siberia the climate is extremely continental.

58751.q: What are the rings of stones and polygons in tundra soil, created by repeated freezing and thawing, called?
58751.e: When it freezes, the water in the ground expands and sorts stones and fine material. This creates regular patterns such as stone rings and polygons.
58751.m: Frost sorts tundra soil into regular patterns.

58752.q: What is the ground in the tundra that stays frozen all year called?
58752.e: Permafrost stays frozen without a break for at least two years. There is also permafrost at high altitudes in the Swiss Alps.

58753.q: Why do many bogs and pools form in the tundra in summer?
a: The meltwater cannot seep away through the frozen ground.
A particularly large amount of rain falls there in summer.
The sea floods the coasts every summer.
58753.e: Only the top layer of soil thaws in summer. Beneath it, the permafrost stays watertight, so the water builds up.
58753.m: In summer, water builds up above the permafrost.

58754.q: Which temperature value characterises the tundra climate according to Köppen?
a: The warmest month averages between 0 and 10 °C.
58754.e: If no month reaches an average of 10 °C, trees can no longer grow. This limit roughly corresponds to the northern tree line.
58754.m: In the tundra, even the warmest month averages less than 10 °C.

58755.q: What is the slow downhill flow of thawed, waterlogged soil over permafrost called?
58755.e: The thawed, wet topsoil slowly slides downhill on the frozen ground beneath. This creates typical tongues of flowing earth.
58755.m: Solifluction is soil flowing over frozen ground.

58756.q: Which animal is particularly important for grazing in the Eurasian tundra and is herded by the Sami?
58756.e: In winter, reindeer feed mainly on reindeer lichen, which they scrape out from under the snow. For peoples such as the Sami, they are the basis of life.
58756.m: Reindeer are the most important grazing animals of the tundra.

58757.q: What is the transition zone between taiga and tundra, with scattered, low-growing trees, called?
58757.e: Towards the north, the trees get smaller and more spread out until they disappear completely at the polar tree line. This transition zone is called forest tundra.
58757.m: The forest tundra links the taiga and the tundra.

58758.q: What danger does thawing permafrost pose for the climate?
a: The greenhouse gases CO2 and methane are released.
More sunlight is reflected by the snow.
It lowers the sea level sharply.
It locks extra CO2 into the soil.
58758.e: Huge amounts of organic material are stored in the permafrost. When it thaws, microorganisms break it down and release greenhouse gases, which increases warming.

58759.q: Why is the prairie in the west of the Great Plains a shortgrass prairie?
a: Little rain falls in the rain shadow of the Rocky Mountains.
The ground there is permanently frozen.
The bison wiped out the tall grass.
It is warmer there than in the east.
58759.e: Rainfall increases from west to east. That is why short grasses grow in the dry west and tallgrass prairie in the wetter east.
58759.m: Towards the west, the prairie gets drier and the grass shorter.

58760.q: Which large animal shaped the North American prairie until it was almost wiped out in the 19th century?
58760.e: Many millions of bison once lived on the prairie. Through mass hunting, their numbers fell to just a few hundred animals by the end of the 19th century.
58760.m: The bison was the defining animal of the prairie.

58761.q: What was the environmental disaster of the 1930s called, when dust storms blew away the farmland soil in the southern Great Plains?
58761.e: Deep ploughing of the prairie destroyed the protective layer of grass. During drought, the wind carried the dried-out soil away, and many farming families had to leave.
58761.m: The Dust Bowl showed how vulnerable ploughed soil is.

58762.q: How is the prairie mainly used today?
a: as farmland for wheat and maize
58762.e: Most of the fertile soils of the prairie have been ploughed up. Today the Wheat Belt and the Corn Belt of the USA are among the most important grain-growing regions in the world.
58762.m: The prairie is now one of the breadbaskets of the world.

58763.q: How do prairie grasses survive drought and fires?
a: They have very deep and dense roots.
They store water in thick leaves.
They shed their roots in summer.
They only grow in the short rainy season.
58763.e: A large part of the plant mass lies underground in the roots. Even if the parts above ground burn or dry up, the grasses sprout again.
58763.m: Prairie grasses survive thanks to deep roots.

58764.q: In which country is most of the Pampas?
58764.e: The Pampas are a wide grassy steppe around Buenos Aires that stretches into Uruguay and southern Brazil.

58765.q: Which large river forms the Río de la Plata together with the Uruguay on the edge of the Pampas?
58765.e: The Río de la Plata is the shared estuary of the Paraná and the Uruguay. Buenos Aires and Montevideo lie on it.
58765.m: The Paraná and the Uruguay flow together into the Río de la Plata.

58766.q: What are the traditional mounted cattle herders of the Pampas called?
58766.e: The gauchos herded huge herds of cattle on the Pampas and are regarded as a symbol of Argentina and Uruguay.
58766.m: Gauchos are the cattle herders of the Pampas.

58767.q: How do the Pampas change from east to west?
58767.e: The humid Pampas in the east are used intensively for arable farming and cattle breeding. Towards the west, rainfall decreases and the dry Pampas turn into steppe.
58767.m: The Pampas get drier and drier towards the west.

58768.q: What climate is found in areas with sclerophyll vegetation?
a: dry, hot summers and mild, wet winters
58768.e: In winter, low-pressure areas of the westerly wind zone bring rain; in summer, subtropical high-pressure areas dominate and bring drought. This climate is called the Mediterranean or etesian climate.
58768.m: Sclerophyll plants grow in a climate with winter rain and dry summers.

58769.q: What are the leaves of sclerophyll plants like?
a: They are small, leathery and have a thick waxy layer.
They are large, thin and soft.
58769.e: The hard, evergreen leaves reduce evaporation during the dry summer. This lets the plants save water even during drought.
58769.m: Leathery, hard leaves protect against water loss.

58770.q: What is the dense, head-high scrubland in the Mediterranean region, which often forms after forests are cut down, called?
58770.e: Maquis consists of evergreen shrubs such as the strawberry tree, tree heath and myrtle. If it continues to be overused, it is reduced to low garrigue.
58770.m: Maquis is dense scrub made up of sclerophyll shrubs.

58771.q: What is the sclerophyll vegetation in California called?
58771.e: Chaparral is a dense, evergreen scrubland. It often burns in dry summers, and many plants are adapted to fire.
58771.m: California’s sclerophyll scrubland is called chaparral.

58772.q: What is the species-rich sclerophyll vegetation in the Cape region of South Africa called?
58772.e: Fynbos is extremely rich in species and typical of the Cape flora. It includes, for example, the proteas.
58772.m: Fynbos is the sclerophyll vegetation of the Cape.

58773.q: Which tree of the Mediterranean region provides cork from its thick bark?
58773.e: The thick bark protects the cork oak from fires and can be stripped every few years without killing the tree. Portugal is the world’s largest producer of cork.
58773.m: Cork comes from the bark of the cork oak.

58774.q: Which sclerophyll tree with evergreen, leathery leaves once formed vast forests in the Mediterranean region?
58774.e: The holm oak is considered a typical tree of the natural sclerophyll forests of the Mediterranean region. Many of these forests have been cut down since ancient times.
58774.m: The holm oak is a typical tree of sclerophyll forests.

58775.q: Where on the continents is sclerophyll vegetation typically found?
a: on the western sides of the continents in the subtropics
on the eastern sides of the continents in the tropics
in the interior of the continents in the polar regions
58775.e: Examples are California, central Chile, the Cape, south-western Australia and the Mediterranean region. There, westerly winds and the subtropical high-pressure area take turns over the year.
58775.m: Sclerophyll areas lie on the subtropical western sides of the continents.

58776.q: Where does the name “laterite” come from?
a: from the Latin word for brick
from the Greek word for earth
from the Portuguese word for red
from the name of a geologist
58776.e: Laterite hardens in the air into a brick-like material. In India and South-East Asia it was therefore cut into blocks and used as a building material.
58776.m: Laterite is named after the Latin word for brick.

58777.q: Which substances build up when laterite forms and give it its red colour?
58777.e: In hot, humid conditions, easily soluble substances such as silica are washed out. What is left are iron and aluminium oxides that hardly dissolve.

58778.q: What happens to laterite when it dries out after the vegetation has been removed?
a: It hardens into a hard crust.
58778.e: Without a protective cover of plants, crust-like layers of laterite can form. These are almost impossible to work and make farming difficult.
58778.m: Exposed laterite can become as hard as stone.

58779.q: Which important raw material for aluminium forms through weathering similar to that of laterite?
58779.e: Bauxite is a particularly aluminium-rich product of weathering in tropical climates. It is the most important raw material for making aluminium.

58780.q: Why are lateritic soils not very productive for farming?
a: They can hardly store any nutrients.
58780.e: Deep weathering has washed out most of the nutrients. The remaining clay minerals such as kaolinite can hold only a few nutrients.
58780.m: Lateritic soils are poor in nutrients.

58781.q: Why does slash-and-burn on tropical laterite soils usually bring good harvests for only a few years?
a: The nutrients from the ash are quickly washed out
The soil freezes in the cool season
The ash poisons the soil permanently
The rain brings too much salt into the fields
58781.e: Laterite soils can hardly store nutrients. The heavy tropical rain quickly washes away the nutrients from the ash, and after that the soil is exhausted.
58781.m: On laterite soils, fertility lasts only a short time after slash-and-burn.

58782.q: Which climatic conditions encourage laterite to form?
a: high temperatures and lots of rain over a long time
58782.e: Warmth speeds up chemical weathering, and lots of seeping water washes out soluble substances. Over millions of years, deep red soils form in this way.
58782.m: Laterite forms in a hot, humid climate over a very long time.

58783.q: In which large regions are deeply weathered red laterite soils particularly widespread?
a: The Amazon Basin and Central Africa
The Sahara and the Arabian Peninsula
58783.e: Laterite soils form in a hot, humid climate over a very long time. Such conditions exist in the always-wet tropics, for example in the Amazon Basin and the Congo Basin.
58783.m: Red laterite soils are typical of the humid tropics.

58784.q: What is the Russian name for black earth?
58784.e: The word means “black earth”. The Russian soil scientist Vasily Dokuchaev described this soil in detail at the end of the 19th century.
58784.m: Chernozem is the Russian word for black earth.

58785.q: From which parent material does black earth usually form?
58785.e: Loess is a fine-grained sediment containing lime that was deposited by the wind. It is loose and rich in minerals and therefore ideal for a fertile soil.
58785.m: Black earth usually develops on loess.

58786.q: Why does so much humus build up in black earth?
a: In the cold winter and dry summer, the litter breaks down only slowly.
Farmers have used a lot of fertiliser for centuries.
58786.e: The steppe grasses provide lots of plant material, which is not completely broken down because of the cold and dryness. Over thousands of years, a very thick layer of humus forms.
58786.m: In the steppe, more humus is built up than broken down.

58787.q: In black earth, what makes sure that humus gets deep into the soil?
a: Burrowing animals such as hamsters and ground squirrels
58787.e: Burrowing animals mix the soil and carry humus down into the depths. Their filled-in tunnels can be seen as patches in the soil profile.
58787.m: Burrowing animals mix up black earth.

58788.q: Which country is known for its large areas of black earth and is often called the “breadbasket of Europe”?
58788.e: Much of Ukraine is covered by fertile black earth. The country is one of the most important exporters of wheat, maize and sunflower oil.
58788.m: Ukraine owes its fertility to black earth.

58789.q: Which German region has particularly fertile black earth soils with top scores in soil assessments?
58789.e: The soils of the Magdeburg Börde score up to 100 points, the highest value, in the official soil assessment. Wheat and sugar beet are grown intensively there.
58789.m: The Magdeburg Börde has Germany’s best soils.

58790.q: In which natural vegetation zone does black earth form?
58790.e: The dense roots of the steppe grasses provide lots of organic material. The continental climate with cold winters and dry summers encourages humus to build up.
58790.m: Black earth is a typical steppe soil.

58791.q: How thick can the humus-rich topsoil layer of a black earth become?
58791.e: The dark A horizon is very thick in typical black earths. Beneath it there is usually loess containing lime.
58791.m: Black earth has a very thick, dark topsoil.

58792.q: What is the lowest, hot altitude zone of the tropical Andes called?
58792.e: The tierra caliente reaches from sea level up to about 800 to 1000 metres. Tropical plants such as bananas, cocoa and sugar cane are grown there.
58792.m: The tierra caliente is the hot lowest zone of the Andes.

58793.q: In which altitude zone of the Andes is coffee mainly grown?
58793.e: The temperate zone lies roughly between 1000 and 2000 to 2500 metres. Coffee thrives there because it is neither too hot nor frosty.
58793.m: Coffee grows in the temperate tierra templada.

58794.q: Which crops are typical of the tierra fría of the Andes?
58794.e: The cool zone lies roughly between 2000 to 2500 and 3500 to 4000 metres. The potato originally comes from the Andes and is well adapted to this climate.
58794.m: Potatoes and cereals grow in the tierra fría.

58795.q: How is the tierra helada of the Andes mainly used?
a: as pasture for llamas and alpacas
58795.e: At great heights, growing crops is hardly possible any more. The grasslands such as the páramo and the puna are used mainly for keeping livestock.
58795.m: Llamas and alpacas graze in the tierra helada.

58796.q: By roughly how many degrees does the temperature in the Andes fall for every 100 metres of altitude?
58796.e: This decrease applies on average to moist air in mountains. Over 3000 metres of altitude, it therefore becomes about 15 to 18 °C cooler.
58796.m: For every 100 metres of altitude, it gets about half a degree cooler.

58797.q: What is the wet high-mountain grassland of the northern Andes in Ecuador and Colombia called?
58797.e: The páramo is cool and wet, often foggy, and stores large amounts of water. Rosette plants such as Espeletia are typical.
58797.m: The páramo is the wet highland of the northern Andes.

58798.q: What is the dry high-mountain grassland of the central Andes in Peru and Bolivia called?
58798.e: The puna lies at about 3500 to 4500 metres and is much drier than the páramo. It is the grazing land of llamas, alpacas and vicuñas.
58798.m: The puna is the dry highland of the central Andes.

58799.q: Which plant from the Andes, which is not a true cereal botanically, is grown on the highlands up to about 4000 metres?
58799.e: Quinoa belongs to the amaranth family, has protein-rich seeds and is very well adapted to cold and drought. It was already a staple food for the Inca.
58799.m: Quinoa is an ancient staple food of the people of the Andes.

58800.q: Which naturalist was the first to describe the altitude zones of vegetation in the Andes in detail, at Chimborazo around 1800?
58800.e: In 1802 Humboldt climbed Chimborazo to a great height. His famous “Tableau physique des Andes” shows the plants in their altitude zones.
58800.m: Alexander von Humboldt explored the altitude zones of the Andes.

58801.q: Which human cause contributes particularly to desertification in the Sahel?
58801.e: If too many animals are kept on one area, they eat away the protective plant cover and trample the soil hard. Wind and heavy rain then carry away the unprotected soil.
58801.m: Too many grazing animals destroy the protective plant cover.

58802.q: What is the UN convention to combat desertification, adopted in 1994, called?
58802.e: The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted on 17 June 1994. Since then, 17 June has been the World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought.
58802.m: The UNCCD is the convention against desertification.

58803.q: What is the large African project that aims to create a wide belt of vegetation right across the Sahel called?
58803.e: The project, launched by the African Union in 2007, aims to restore land along a length of about 8000 kilometres. Besides trees, it also includes pastures and farmland.
58803.m: The Great Green Wall is meant to make the Sahel green again.

58804.q: How can irrigation projects in dry areas contribute to desertification?
a: Salts build up in the soil through evaporation.
The water cools the soil too much.
The groundwater is refilled too much.
58804.e: With high evaporation, the salts dissolved in the water stay behind in the topsoil. Salty soils become infertile and often have to be abandoned.
58804.m: Wrong irrigation can make soils salty.

58805.q: Which simple technique do farmers in the Sahel use to hold rainwater on the field?
a: Rows of stones along the contour lines
Burning the fields before the rain
Removing all the trees from the field
58805.e: The low stone walls slow down the water running off, so that it can seep in. At the same time they hold back fertile soil.
58805.m: Rows of stones keep water and soil on the field.

58806.q: What are zaï pits, which are used in the Sahel against land degradation?
a: small planting holes that collect water and fertiliser
58806.e: Manure or compost is put into the small pits and seeds are sown. They catch the rainwater and make crusted soils usable again.
58806.m: Zaï pits collect water and nutrients for the plants.

58807.q: Why does collecting firewood contribute to desertification?
a: Without trees and shrubs, the soil is worn away more easily.
Firewood removes salt from the soil.
Collecting wood raises the water table.
58807.e: Many people in dry areas cook with wood. If trees and shrubs disappear faster than they grow back, there is no protection against wind and water erosion.
58807.m: Without trees and shrubs, the soil loses its protection.

58808.q: Why does slash-and-burn only provide good harvests for a short time?
a: The nutrients from the ash are quickly washed out.
The soil freezes after the fire.
The ash is poisonous for crops.
The fire kills all pollinating insects for good.
58808.e: The ash fertilises the soil for a short time. But heavy rain quickly washes out the nutrients, so yields fall sharply after a few years.
58808.m: Fertilising with ash only lasts a short time.

58809.q: What is the traditional way of farming called in which farmers move on with their whole settlement after slash-and-burn?
58809.e: In shifting cultivation, people move both their fields and their settlement. In rotational bush fallow, the settlement stays where it is and only the fields change.
58809.m: In shifting cultivation, fields and settlement move on.

58810.q: What is the form of slash-and-burn farming called in which the settlement stays and only the fields change?
58810.e: The fields are abandoned after a few years and become overgrown again, while the village community stays in the same place. After a long fallow period, an area can be cleared again.
58810.m: In rotational bush fallow, only the fields change.

58811.q: Why does traditional slash-and-burn become a problem as the population grows?
a: The fallow periods become too short for the forest to recover.
The fields become too big for irrigation.
The ash is no longer enough for building houses.
There is not enough seed for the fields.
58811.e: For soil and forest to regenerate, many years of fallow are needed. If areas are used again too soon, the soils become poor for good.
58811.m: Slash-and-burn is only sustainable with a long fallow period.

58812.q: Which land use is the main reason for forest clearing in the Brazilian Amazon today?
58812.e: Large parts of the cleared areas become cattle pasture. Growing soya also plays an important role.
58812.m: Cattle pastures are the main reason for clearing in the Amazon.

58813.q: What effect does slash-and-burn have on the climate?
a: CO2 that was stored in trees is released.
Extra oxygen is released into the atmosphere.
The ozone layer is built up.
The smoke cools the Earth permanently.
58813.e: When biomass is burned, carbon enters the atmosphere as CO2. In addition, the forest is then missing as a carbon store.

58814.q: For which plantations are large areas of rainforest being cleared in Indonesia and Malaysia?
58814.e: Palm oil is used in many foods and cosmetics and as fuel. The fires used for clearing at times cause heavy smoke pollution in South-East Asia.
58814.m: Rainforest is being cleared in South-East Asia for oil palm plantations.

58815.q: What is slash-and-burn clearing with a later change of fields called in English?
58815.e: The term describes a way of using land in which fields are left to return to forest after a few years of use. Millions of people around the world live from this form of farming.
58815.m: Shifting cultivation is the English term for the German Wanderfeldbau.

58816.q: Where are most of the nutrients stored in the tropical rainforest?
a: in the thick layer of humus
58816.e: The soil itself is poor and can hardly hold nutrients. Almost all the nutrients are in the plants and are taken up again straight away when they die.
58816.m: In the rainforest, the nutrients are in the plants, not in the soil.

58817.q: Why is the litter layer in the tropical rainforest so thin?
a: Warmth and moisture speed up decomposition greatly.
The wind blows the leaves away.
The rain washes the leaves into the sea.
58817.e: Fungi, bacteria, termites and other decomposers break down the leaves in a few weeks to months. That is why hardly any humus layer forms.
58817.m: In the rainforest, leaves decompose very quickly.

58818.q: Which living things help rainforest trees to take up nutrients directly from the litter?
58818.e: The fungi live in symbiosis with the tree roots and unlock nutrients from the decomposed litter. This means hardly any nutrients are lost by being washed out.
58818.m: Mycorrhizal fungi supply the trees directly with nutrients.

58819.q: What is the nutrient cycle in the tropical rainforest called, because nutrients hardly reach the soil?
58819.e: The nutrients from the litter are taken up again directly by the plants. The mineral soil hardly plays a role in this.
58819.m: The rainforest has a short-circuited nutrient cycle.

58820.q: What happens to the nutrients when large areas of rainforest are cleared?
a: They are washed out by heavy rain.
They build up in the soil.
They stay in the litter for decades.
They are locked up by permafrost.
58820.e: Without plants, the cycle is broken, and the nutrient-poor soil cannot hold the substances released. That is why reforestation is very difficult.
58820.m: After clearing, the rainforest’s nutrients are lost.

58821.q: What is the fertile dark earth in the Amazon region called, which was created by people and contains a lot of charcoal?
58821.e: Centuries ago, Indigenous communities enriched the soil with charcoal, bones and waste. These soils are still much more fertile than the surrounding area today.
58821.m: Terra preta is a man-made fertile earth in the Amazon.

58822.q: Why do most rainforest trees have very shallow roots?
a: The nutrients are only in the top layer of soil.
The ground beneath is permanently frozen.
It is too dry in the subsoil.
Deep roots would be eaten by animals.
58822.e: Because the nutrients come from the decomposed litter, it pays for the trees to spread their fine roots just below the surface. There is plenty of water anyway.
58822.m: Rainforest trees get their nutrients just below the surface.

58823.q: What does a comparison between tropical rainforest and Central European broadleaf forest show about nutrient storage?
a: In broadleaf forest, a larger share of the nutrients is stored in the soil.
In rainforest, more humus is stored in the soil.
Both store nutrients in the same way.
In broadleaf forest, there are no nutrients in the soil.
58823.e: In temperate latitudes, decomposition is slower, and humus and clay minerals hold nutrients in the soil. As a result, the soils stay fertile even after clearing.
58823.m: Soils in temperate latitudes store more nutrients than tropical ones.

58824.q: Which two properties of seawater drive the thermohaline circulation?
a: Tides and the position of the Moon
58824.e: “Thermo” stands for temperature, “haline” for salt. Both determine the density of the water, and denser water sinks.
58824.m: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks into the depths.

58825.q: In which sea areas does North Atlantic Deep Water mainly sink?
a: Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico
Gulf of Guinea and Sargasso Sea
58825.e: In the far north, the salty surface water cools down strongly, becomes heavy and sinks into the depths. This is where North Atlantic Deep Water forms.
58825.m: North Atlantic Deep Water forms in the far north of the Atlantic.

58826.q: Because of its worldwide cycle, what is the thermohaline circulation often called as an image?
58826.e: The oceanographer Wallace Broecker made the image of the “conveyor belt” well known. It links all ocean basins in a cycle of surface and deep currents.
58826.m: The thermohaline circulation works like a global conveyor belt.

58827.q: Why does the formation of sea ice increase the salt content of the surrounding water?
a: Most of the salt is pushed out during freezing
The ice dissolves extra salt from the seabed
The ice attracts salt from the air
A particularly large amount of water evaporates under the ice
58827.e: Sea ice consists mostly of fresh water; the salt stays behind in the sea as brine. The saltier, cold water becomes heavier and sinks.
58827.m: Freezing seawater leaves its salt behind in the ocean.

58828.q: Roughly how long does a complete circuit of water in the global conveyor belt take?
58828.e: Deep water moves very slowly. A whole circuit is reckoned to take about a thousand years.
58828.m: One circuit of the global conveyor belt takes about a thousand years.

58829.q: Which abbreviation stands for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation?
58829.e: AMOC stands for “Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation”. It carries warm water north and cold deep water south.
58829.m: The AMOC is the Atlantic part of the overturning circulation.

58830.q: How does the amount of water carried by the Gulf Stream compare with the amount of water in all the rivers on Earth put together?
a: It is about half as large
It is only a small fraction of it
58830.e: Oceanographers measure such currents in sverdrups; 1 sverdrup equals one million cubic metres per second. Depending on the section, the Gulf Stream carries 30 to over 100 sverdrups, while all the rivers on Earth together carry only just over 1 sverdrup.
58830.m: Ocean currents move much more water than all the rivers together.

58831.q: Where does Antarctic Bottom Water, the densest water mass in the world’s oceans, form?
a: In the Weddell Sea and the Ross Sea
58831.e: Off Antarctica, water cools down extremely and becomes saltier through the formation of sea ice. It sinks to the seabed and spreads northwards.
58831.m: Antarctic Bottom Water forms mainly in the Weddell Sea.

58832.q: Why could strong melting of the Greenland ice weaken the overturning circulation in the Atlantic?
a: Fresh water lowers the density of the surface water
Meltwater greatly increases the salt content
The ice cools the Atlantic to zero degrees
58832.e: Fresh water dilutes the salty surface water. It becomes lighter and sinks less easily, which weakens what drives the circulation.
58832.m: A lot of meltwater can slow down the sinking in the North Atlantic.

58833.q: At which phases of the Moon does a spring tide occur?
a: At new moon and full moon
58833.e: At new and full moon, the sun, Earth and Moon are almost in a line. Their tidal forces add up, and the tidal range is particularly large.
58833.m: Spring tides occur when the sun, Moon and Earth are in a line.

58834.q: What is the tide with a particularly small tidal range, which occurs at half moon, called?
58834.e: At half moon, the sun and Moon are at right angles as seen from the Earth. Their tidal forces partly cancel each other out.
58834.m: At half moon there are only weak neap tides.

58835.q: With semi-diurnal tides, roughly how much time passes between two high tides?
58835.e: A lunar day lasts about 24 hours 50 minutes, and there are two high tides in it. Half of that gives about 12 hours 25 minutes.
58835.m: Two high tides follow each other just over twelve hours apart.

58836.q: Why do the times of high and low tide shift by about 50 minutes every day?
a: The Moon is over the same place later each day
The Earth turns more slowly every day
The sun slows the water down every day
The wind delays the high tide every day
58836.e: The Moon moves along its orbit in the same direction as the Earth turns. That is why a place needs about 50 minutes longer each day before it is under the Moon again.
58836.m: The tides follow the lunar day, not the solar day.

58837.q: In which country is the tidal power station at Lake Sihwa, the largest in the world by output?
58837.e: The power station went into operation in 2011 and has an output of about 254 megawatts. It uses an existing dam that cuts off an arm of the sea.
58837.m: The world’s largest tidal power station is in South Korea.

58838.q: What is a point in the ocean called where the tidal range is almost zero and around which the tidal wave circles?
58838.e: Because of the Earth’s rotation and the shape of the ocean basins, tidal waves rotate around such points. At their centre, the water level hardly rises or falls.
58838.m: At an amphidromic point there is almost no tidal range.

58839.q: Because of tidal interaction, roughly how far does the Moon move away from the Earth every year?
58839.e: The distance is measured very precisely with laser beams aimed at reflectors placed by Apollo astronauts. The value is just under 4 centimetres per year.
58839.m: The Moon moves a few centimetres further away from the Earth every year.

58840.q: What long-term effect does tidal friction have on the Earth?
a: The Earth’s rotation slows down and the days get longer
The Earth turns faster and faster
The Moon moves closer to the Earth
58840.e: The friction of the tidal currents slows down the Earth’s rotation. In the process, angular momentum is transferred to the Moon, which slowly moves away from the Earth.
58840.m: Tidal friction is gradually making the Earth’s days longer.

58841.q: Why is the tidal range in the Mediterranean usually only small?
a: It is almost enclosed and only narrowly connected to the Atlantic
The Moon has a weaker effect there than elsewhere
Its water is too salty for tides
It is too close to the equator
58841.e: The Atlantic tidal wave can hardly get in through the narrow Strait of Gibraltar. The basin itself is too small for strong tides of its own.
58841.m: Because it is almost enclosed, the Mediterranean has only small tides.

58842.q: Roughly how strong is the Moon’s tide-producing force compared with that of the sun?
58842.e: Tidal force decreases with the cube of the distance. The Moon is much lighter than the sun, but so much closer that its effect is about 2.2 times greater.
58842.m: The Moon produces tides about twice as strong as the sun’s.

58843.q: What does the flow regime of a river describe?
a: The typical pattern of flow over the year
The length of the river’s course
The flow speed during a flood
The chemical quality of the water
58843.e: The flow regime shows in which months a river carries a lot or little water on long-term average. It depends on rainfall, snow, glaciers and evaporation.
58843.m: The flow regime shows a river’s typical water level over the year.

58844.q: In which months does a glacial flow regime in the Alps reach its maximum?
58844.e: Glaciers melt most in midsummer, when it is warmest. In winter, by contrast, such rivers carry very little water.
58844.m: Glacier rivers carry the most water in midsummer.

58845.q: What mainly shapes a nival flow regime?
58845.e: “Nival” comes from the Latin “nix” for snow. The maximum is usually in late spring or early summer, when the snow melts.
58845.m: A nival regime is determined by snowmelt.
