58846.q: In June, a river carries on average twice as much water as its annual average. What value do you get when you divide the monthly flow by the annual flow?
58846.e: Dividing the average monthly flow by the average annual flow gives the Pardé coefficient. Values above 1 show months with a lot of water, values below 1 months with little water.
58846.m: The Pardé coefficient compares each month with the annual average.

58847.q: Which flow regime do rivers on the Swiss Plateau and in the Jura have, whose flow depends mainly on rain?
58847.e: “Pluvial” comes from the Latin “pluvia” for rain. Such rivers often have higher flows in winter and spring and low ones in late summer.
58847.m: Rivers shaped by rain have a pluvial regime.

58848.q: Why is the flow of the Rhine below Lake Constance more even than above it?
a: The lake stores floodwater and releases it later
The lake immediately evaporates excess water
Most of the water seeps away in the lake
The lake diverts floodwater into the Danube
58848.e: Large lakes act as buffers. They soften flow peaks and increase the flow in dry periods.
58848.m: Lakes even out the flow of a river.

58849.q: What is the graph of the flow at a gauging station over time called?
58849.e: A hydrograph shows the flow or water level over time. During a flood, you can see the rise, peak and fall on it.
58849.m: A hydrograph shows the flow over time.

58850.q: In the long term, how does glacier retreat affect the summer flow of rivers shaped by glaciers?
a: The winter flow falls to zero
The river freezes over in summer
The regime becomes more and more glacial
58850.e: At first, melting glaciers supply more water. As they get smaller, this source is missing, and the rivers carry less water in midsummer.
58850.m: In the long run, shrinking glaciers supply less summer water.

58851.q: Which federal body runs Switzerland’s national network of river flow measuring stations?
a: Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology (MeteoSwiss)
58851.e: The FOEN’s hydrology division measures water level and flow at many stations. From these long series of measurements, the flow regimes of Swiss rivers can be determined.
58851.m: The FOEN measures the flow of Swiss rivers.

58852.q: What is the boundary line between two neighbouring river basins called?
58852.e: The watershed usually runs along ridges and crests. Rain that falls on different sides flows into different river systems.
58852.m: A watershed separates two river basins.

58853.q: Which river has the largest drainage basin in the world?
58853.e: The Amazon’s drainage basin covers about 6 to 7 million square kilometres. That is about 40 per cent of the area of South America.
58853.m: The Amazon has the largest drainage basin on Earth.

58854.q: The drainage basins of three Swiss rivers meet at the Witenwasserenstock. Which ones?
58854.e: The peak is in the Gotthard area. From here, water flows via the Reuss to the Rhine, via the Rhône to the Mediterranean and via the Ticino to the Po.
58854.m: The Reuss, Rhône and Ticino divide at the Witenwasserenstock.

58855.q: At Piz Lunghin in the Upper Engadine, the drainage basins of three seas meet. Which ones?
a: North Sea, Adriatic and Black Sea
North Sea, Baltic Sea and Adriatic
Mediterranean, Baltic Sea and Black Sea
North Sea, Atlantic and Baltic Sea
58855.e: From Piz Lunghin, water flows via the Rhine into the North Sea, via the Maira and Po into the Adriatic and via the Inn and Danube into the Black Sea. It is called a triple watershed.
58855.m: At Piz Lunghin, the water divides between three seas.

58856.q: What is an endorheic drainage basin?
a: An area with no outflow to the sea
An area that only carries groundwater
An area that drains into two seas
58856.e: In an area with no outflow, the water ends in an inland lake or a basin. There it evaporates or seeps away.
58856.m: An endorheic area has no outflow to the ocean.

58857.q: Which body of water is the largest inland body of water with no outflow on Earth?
58857.e: The Caspian Sea has no natural outflow to the ocean. Its most important inflow is the Volga.
58857.m: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake with no outflow to the sea.

58858.q: What is the flow per unit area of a drainage basin called, usually given in litres per second per square kilometre?
58858.e: Specific discharge makes drainage basins of different sizes comparable. In the Alps it is much larger than in the lowlands because of the high rainfall.
58858.m: Specific discharge shows how much water each square kilometre supplies.

58859.q: Through which river does most of the Engadine drain?
58859.e: The Inn flows from the Engadine to Austria and joins the Danube at Passau. This means the Engadine is part of the Black Sea’s drainage basin.
58859.m: The Engadine drains via the Inn to the Danube.

58860.q: Why are the size, shape and gradient of a drainage basin important for flood protection?
a: They determine how much water reaches the outlet and how fast
They determine the temperature of the river water
They determine the salt content of the river
They determine the number of fish species
58860.e: A small, steep and roundish area lets rainfall flow together quickly. This creates high, short flood peaks.
58860.m: Steep and compact drainage basins react quickly to heavy rain.

58861.q: What is a layer of rock that can store groundwater and pass it on called?
58861.e: An aquifer has enough spaces such as pores or cracks. An aquiclude such as clay, by contrast, hardly lets any water through.
58861.m: An aquifer stores groundwater and passes it on.

58862.q: Roughly what percentage of drinking water in Switzerland comes from groundwater, including springs?
58862.e: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, about 80 per cent of drinking water comes from groundwater. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
58862.m: Most Swiss drinking water is groundwater.

58863.q: Why is groundwater in the karst limestone of the Jura particularly vulnerable to pollution?
a: It flows quickly through cracks and is hardly filtered
The limestone makes the water poisonous
It always lies directly beneath fields
58863.e: In limestone, water dissolves caves and cracks. Groundwater often flows quickly through them without being cleaned as it would be in sand and gravel.
58863.m: Karst groundwater flows quickly and is therefore sensitive to pollution.

a: A well from which groundwater under pressure comes out by itself
A well that only delivers water with a pump
A well that collects only rainwater
A well that takes in seawater
58864.e: If an aquifer lies beneath a watertight layer and its catchment area is higher up, the water is under pressure. When a hole is drilled, it then rises by itself to above the surface.
58864.m: Water gushes out of an artesian well by itself.

58865.q: What mainly determines how fast groundwater flows through the ground?
a: The permeability of the rock and the gradient
The air temperature above the ground
58865.e: Groundwater flows much faster through coarse gravel than through fine clay. It also flows faster the steeper the slope of the water table. Henry Darcy described this in 1856.
58865.m: Permeability and gradient determine how fast groundwater flows.

58866.q: Which large aquifer beneath the Great Plains of the USA is heavily overused for irrigation?
58866.e: The Ogallala Aquifer lies beneath eight states. Because far more water is taken out than is replenished, water levels are falling in many places.
58866.m: The Ogallala Aquifer is being emptied faster than it refills.

58867.q: What is meant by fossil groundwater?
a: Very old groundwater that is hardly replenished
58867.e: Fossil groundwater often formed thousands of years ago during wetter climate periods, for example under the Sahara. Anyone who uses it is depleting a reserve.
58867.m: Fossil groundwater is a reserve that does not refill.

58868.q: Which land use is a main source of nitrate in groundwater?
58868.e: Fertiliser and liquid manure contain nitrogen, which can be washed into groundwater as nitrate. That is why areas with a lot of arable farming are particularly affected.
58868.m: Too much fertiliser pollutes groundwater with nitrate.

58869.q: What is it called when drinking water is obtained from wells near a river, with river water seeping through the ground?
58869.e: The river water is cleaned on its way through gravel and sand. Many cities, including in Switzerland, use groundwater enriched in this way.
58869.m: In riverbank filtration, the ground cleans the river water.

58870.q: Which former island in the Aral Sea served the Soviet Union as a testing ground for biological weapons?
58870.e: The island had a secret laboratory and testing ground. As the water level fell, it became a peninsula around 2001, which raised fears about buried pathogens.
58870.m: Vozrozhdeniya Island was a secret biological weapons testing ground.

58871.q: To grow which crop was water mainly taken from the rivers feeding the Aral Sea in Soviet times?
58871.e: The Soviet Union built huge irrigated areas in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. Cotton was regarded as “white gold”.
58871.m: Irrigating cotton made the Aral Sea dry up.

58872.q: Until the early 1960s, where did the Aral Sea rank by area among the world's inland lakes?
58872.e: At around 68,000 square kilometres, it was about the size of Ireland. Since then it has lost most of its area.
58872.m: The Aral Sea was once the fourth largest inland lake in the world.

58873.q: Which dam, completed in 2005, stabilises the North Aral Sea?
58873.e: The dam in Kazakhstan stops the water of the Syr Darya flowing away into the southern part. The northern part rose again and fishing partly recovered.
58873.m: The Kokaral Dam saved the small Aral Sea.

58874.q: Around 2002, how salty was the water in the western part of the Large Aral Sea compared with seawater?
58874.e: Originally the lake contained only about 10 grams of salt per litre. Through evaporation the value in the western basin rose to over 80 grams by 2002, so most fish species disappeared.
58874.m: As it dried up, the Aral Sea became extremely salty.

58875.q: Which former port town in Uzbekistan is known for its “ship graveyard” in the sand?
58875.e: Moynaq used to lie right on the shore and lived from fishing. Today the water is many dozens of kilometres away, and rusty ships lie in the sand.
58875.m: In Moynaq, ships lie in the middle of the desert.

58876.q: Which two countries share the Aral Sea?
58876.e: The northern part lies in Kazakhstan, the southern part in Uzbekistan. The rivers feeding it also cross other Central Asian countries.
58876.m: The Aral Sea lies between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

58877.q: What health hazard does the dried-up lake bed pose to people living nearby?
a: Dust containing salt and pesticides is blown around
Radioactive radiation from the lake water
Poisonous volcanic gases from the ground
58877.e: Storms carry salt and pesticide residues from irrigation far inland. Respiratory diseases are increasingly common in the region.
58877.m: The dust of the Aral Sea makes people ill.

58878.q: How did the regional climate around the Aral Sea change as it dried up?
a: It became more continental, with hotter summers and colder winters
It became wetter, with more rain
It became more oceanic, with milder winters
58878.e: A large body of water stores heat and evens out temperatures. Without this buffer, the contrasts between summer and winter become greater.
58878.m: Without the Aral Sea, the region's climate has become more extreme.

58879.q: On which river is the Three Gorges Dam?
58879.e: The dam holds back the Yangtze, the longest river in China and Asia. The name comes from three gorges upstream of the wall.
58879.m: The Three Gorges Dam holds back the Yangtze.

58880.q: What is the installed capacity of the Three Gorges Dam hydropower station?
58880.e: It has 32 turbines of 700 megawatts each and 2 smaller ones of 50 megawatts each. This makes it the most powerful power station in the world (as of 2025).
58880.m: The Three Gorges power station is the most powerful power station on Earth (as of 2025).

58881.q: Which major city lies at the upper end of the Three Gorges reservoir?
58881.e: The reservoir stretches about 600 kilometres upstream to the region of the city of Chongqing, home to millions. Since then, large ships have been able to sail all the way there.
58881.m: The Three Gorges reservoir reaches as far as Chongqing.

58882.q: Roughly how many people had to be resettled for the Three Gorges reservoir?
58882.e: Entire towns and villages were flooded and rebuilt. Some estimates even put the number affected higher.
58882.m: Over a million people lost their homes for the Three Gorges reservoir.

58883.q: What effect did the Three Gorges Dam have on shipping on the Yangtze?
a: Larger ships can sail further upstream
Only rowing boats may use the river
The river has no longer been navigable since
58883.e: The reservoir flooded rapids and narrow gorges. With locks and a ship lift, large ships now reach Chongqing.
58883.m: The reservoir made the Yangtze easier for large ships to navigate.

58884.q: In which year was the wall of the Three Gorges Dam completed?
58884.e: Construction began in 1994/1995, and the wall was finished in May 2006. Further parts of the power station followed, and the ship lift went into operation in 2016.
58884.m: The Three Gorges wall was completed in 2006.

58885.q: Besides generating electricity, which purpose of the Three Gorges Dam is particularly important?
a: Flood protection along the middle and lower river
58885.e: Hundreds of thousands of people died in floods on the Yangtze in the 20th century. The reservoir can hold back flood peaks.
58885.m: The Three Gorges Dam is meant to tame floods on the Yangtze.

58886.q: What problem arises because the Three Gorges reservoir holds back sediment?
a: Mud is missing downstream, and the delta erodes
The water downstream becomes saltier than seawater
The river downstream freezes over in winter
The turbines produce more electricity as a result
58886.e: The Yangtze used to carry a lot of suspended material to its mouth. Without this supply, the banks and delta no longer grow.
58886.m: Reservoirs hold back sediment that is then missing downstream.

58887.q: How do ships overcome the large difference in height at the Three Gorges Dam?
a: With flights of locks and a ship lift
With a tunnel under the dam wall
With cranes that lift each ship individually
58887.e: Two flights of locks with several chambers raise large ships in stages. Since 2016, a ship lift has raised smaller ships in a few minutes.
58887.m: Locks and a ship lift take ships over the dam wall.

58888.q: The concept of virtual water was developed in the 1990s using the example of which world region?
58888.e: The British geographer Tony Allan studied how water-scarce countries in the Middle East “import” water through grain imports. He received the Stockholm Water Prize for this in 2008.
58888.m: The concept of virtual water arose from the example of the water-scarce Middle East.

58889.q: What is meant by virtual water?
a: Water that was used to make a product
Water that only exists in computer simulations
58889.e: Virtual water is not visibly contained in the product, but it was used up in growing or making it. When the product is traded, the water is indirectly exported too.
58889.m: Every product contains invisible virtual water.

58890.q: On global average, roughly how much virtual water is contained in one kilogram of beef?
58890.e: Most of it is in the feed the cattle eat during their lives. That is why meat needs much more water than grain.
58890.m: Beef has a very high water requirement.

58891.q: What is the name of the measure developed by Arjen Hoekstra around 2002 for the total water use of a person or country?
58891.e: The water footprint adds together direct use and the virtual water in the goods consumed. It is divided into green, blue and grey water.
58891.m: The water footprint also measures the water in our shopping.

58892.q: In the water footprint, what does “green water” mean?
a: Rainwater in the soil that plants take up
Water from rivers and groundwater used for irrigation
58892.e: Green water comes directly from rainfall and is stored in the soil. Plants take it up and release it again through evaporation.
58892.m: Green water is rainwater that plants use.

58893.q: In the water footprint, what does “grey water” mean?
a: Water from lakes used for irrigation
Treated waste water from sewage works
58893.e: Grey water is a notional amount. It shows how much clean water would be needed to dilute pollutants below the limit values.
58893.m: Grey water measures pollution as an amount of water.

58894.q: In the water footprint, what does “blue water” mean?
a: Surface water and groundwater that is taken and used up
Rainwater that soaks directly into the ground
58894.e: Blue water is taken from rivers, lakes or groundwater, for example for irrigation. Afterwards it is no longer available to other users in the catchment area.
58894.m: Blue water is taken from rivers, lakes and groundwater.

58895.q: According to a 2012 study, what percentage of Switzerland's water footprint arises abroad?
58895.e: The study commissioned by the SDC came to 82 percent. The reason is imported food, clothing and other goods.
58895.m: Most of Switzerland's water use is contained in imports.

58896.q: Why can it make sense for a very dry country to import grain rather than grow it itself?
a: It saves its own scarce water
Grain does not grow in deserts
58896.e: With the grain, the water needed to grow it is imported virtually. The country's own water remains available for households and industry.
58896.m: A desert country can save water by importing grain.

58897.q: According to the Falkenmark indicator, below what amount of renewable water per person per year do we speak of water stress?
58897.e: The Swedish hydrologist Malin Falkenmark set this threshold. Less water per person regularly leads to supply problems.
58897.m: Below 1700 cubic metres per person per year, there is water stress.

58898.q: According to the Falkenmark indicator, what is a situation with less than 500 cubic metres of water per person per year called?
58898.e: Below 1000 cubic metres we speak of water scarcity, below 500 of absolute scarcity. Then there is barely enough water for basic needs and farming.
58898.m: Below 500 cubic metres per person, there is absolute water scarcity.

58899.q: Which sector takes the most fresh water worldwide?
58899.e: About 70 percent of global freshwater withdrawals go into irrigation. That is why efficient irrigation is key to fighting water stress.
58899.m: Agriculture is the biggest water user in the world.

58900.q: Which city announced a possible “Day Zero” in 2018, when the taps would be turned off?
58900.e: After several years of drought, the reservoirs were almost empty. Strict saving measures and rain prevented Day Zero.
58900.m: In 2018 Cape Town narrowly avoided a day without tap water.

58901.q: What does the water stress indicator in UN Sustainable Development Goal 6 measure?
a: Freshwater withdrawal relative to available renewable resources
The number of wells per inhabitant
The price of water per cubic metre
The length of water pipes per country
58901.e: Indicator 6.4.2 compares withdrawals with renewable fresh water, minus what ecosystems need. The higher the share, the greater the stress.
58901.m: Water stress arises when a large part of the available water is taken.

58902.q: What does it mean if a country has “extremely high” water stress according to the Aqueduct atlas?
a: It uses most of its available water every year
It has severe floods every year
Its drinking water is heavily polluted
It has to import all its water
58902.e: If more than four fifths of the available water is used every year, there is hardly any reserve left for drought years. Many countries in the Middle East are in this class.
58902.m: Extremely high water stress means almost all available water is used.

58903.q: According to analyses by the World Resources Institute, which world region is most affected by water stress?
58903.e: Rainfall there is low, evaporation is high and the population is growing. Many countries take almost all the available water or more.
58903.m: The Middle East and North Africa suffer most from water stress.

58904.q: What is meant by economic water scarcity?
a: Water is available, but money and infrastructure to use it are lacking
Water is too expensive for factories in rich countries
Nature basically provides too little water
Water is traded on the stock exchange
58904.e: Many regions in sub-Saharan Africa have enough rainfall. But they lack pipes, storage and treatment to bring the water to people.
58904.m: Economic water scarcity comes from a lack of infrastructure.

58905.q: Which Indian city of millions had a severe water crisis in 2019 because its four main reservoirs were almost empty?
58905.e: After a weak monsoon and overuse of groundwater, Chennai had to bring in water by train and tanker lorry. The crisis showed the consequences of water stress in fast-growing cities.
58905.m: Chennai had a major water crisis in 2019.

58906.q: Which method of seawater desalination is the most widespread worldwide today?
58906.e: Reverse osmosis needs less energy than thermal methods. That is why most new plants are built using it today.
58906.m: Reverse osmosis is the most important desalination method.

a: High pressure forces water through a membrane, and the salt stays behind
Seawater is boiled and the steam condenses
Salt is pulled out of the water with magnets
Seawater is frozen and the ice is melted
58907.e: The pressure must exceed the osmotic pressure of the salt water. The semi-permeable membrane lets water molecules through but not dissolved salts.
58907.m: In reverse osmosis, water is pushed through a fine membrane.

58908.q: Which thermal method evaporates seawater in many stages, each at lower pressure?
58908.e: As the pressure drops, the preheated seawater boils again in each stage. The method is common mainly around the Persian Gulf, where energy is cheap.
58908.m: Thermal desalination uses evaporation at low pressure.

58909.q: What is the main environmental problem of seawater desalination?
a: The very salty brine that is returned to the sea
That the sea becomes less salty
58909.e: The brine is much saltier and often warmer than seawater and can contain chemicals. On the seabed it harms plants and animals.
58909.m: The brine from desalination plants pollutes the sea.

58910.q: What is the average salt content of seawater?
58910.e: That is about 3.5 percent. Drinking water may contain only a fraction of that.
58910.m: Seawater contains on average about 35 grams of salt per litre.

58911.q: Roughly how much electrical energy does a modern reverse osmosis plant need per cubic metre of drinking water from seawater?
58911.e: Thanks to energy recovery, the requirement has fallen sharply. Thermal methods need considerably more energy.
58911.m: Modern reverse osmosis needs only a few kilowatt hours per cubic metre.

58912.q: Which country produces the most desalinated seawater in the world?
58912.e: Saudi Arabia has hardly any rivers and hardly any renewable groundwater. Large plants such as Ras Al-Khair supply millions of people.
58912.m: Saudi Arabia is the largest producer of desalinated water.

58913.q: Why are minerals usually added back to water after reverse osmosis?
a: It is so low in minerals that it attacks pipes and tastes flat
It still contains too much salt
58913.e: Almost pure water is aggressive and can corrode metal pipes. So lime, for example, is added, which also helps the taste.
58913.m: Desalinated water needs some lime added again.

58914.q: According to a 2019 study, on average how much brine is produced worldwide per litre of desalinated water?
58914.e: The study counted about 16,000 plants. Every day they produced about 95 million cubic metres of fresh water and about 142 million cubic metres of brine.
58914.m: Desalination produces more brine than drinking water.

58915.q: On which river is the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam?
58915.e: The Blue Nile rises from Lake Tana in the Ethiopian Highlands. It joins the White Nile in Khartoum.
58915.m: Ethiopia's great dam holds back the Blue Nile.

58916.q: When was the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam officially inaugurated?
58916.e: The inauguration took place on 9 September 2025, after about 14 years of construction. In Ethiopia it is seen as a national prestige project.
58916.m: Ethiopia inaugurated its great Nile dam in 2025.

58917.q: What is the installed capacity of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam power station?
58917.e: Originally 6000 megawatts were planned, but the number of turbines was reduced to 13. The power station is meant to ease the country's electricity shortage.
58917.m: The Renaissance Dam has a capacity of just over 5000 megawatts.

58918.q: Which two downstream countries fear disadvantages from the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam?
58918.e: Egypt covers almost all its water needs from the Nile. Both countries demand binding rules for filling and operating the dam, especially in drought years.
58918.m: Egypt and Sudan are worried about their Nile water.

58919.q: What record does the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam power station hold?
a: Highest dam wall in the world
Oldest power station on the Nile
58919.e: Its capacity exceeds all other hydropower stations on the continent. The dam wall itself, at 145 metres, is not record-breakingly high.
58919.m: The Renaissance Dam has the largest hydropower station in Africa.

58920.q: In which region of Ethiopia is the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam?
a: Benishangul-Gumuz, near the border with Sudan
Tigray, near the border with Eritrea
Somali, near the border with Somalia
58920.e: The dam is in the west of the country, only about 10 to 20 kilometres from the Sudanese border. There the Blue Nile flows from the highlands into the lowlands.
58920.m: The Renaissance Dam lies in western Ethiopia near Sudan.

58921.q: How was the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam mainly financed?
a: Mostly from its own funds, including bonds sold to the public
58921.e: Ethiopia sold government bonds to its citizens and collected contributions from public employees. Loans from Chinese banks were also used for turbines and electrical equipment.
58921.m: Ethiopia largely financed its great dam itself.

58922.q: Roughly how much water can the reservoir of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam hold?
58922.e: That is roughly one and a half times the annual flow of the Blue Nile. That is why the speed of filling is so controversial for the downstream countries.
58922.m: The reservoir in Ethiopia holds about 74 cubic kilometres of water.

58923.q: In which year did filling of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam reservoir begin?
58923.e: The first filling took place in July 2020 during the rainy season. After that the lake was filled further in several yearly steps.
58923.m: Filling of the Ethiopian Nile reservoir began in 2020.

58924.q: What does the demographic transition model describe?
a: The change from high to low birth and death rates
The migration of the rural population to the cities
The shift of workers into the service sector
The change from agricultural to industrial societies in world trade
58924.e: The model describes how a society moves from high to low birth and death rates as it modernises. In between, the population grows strongly.
58924.m: The demographic transition leads from high to low birth and death rates.

58925.q: What characterises the first (pre-transition) stage of the demographic transition?
a: High birth rates and high death rates
High birth rates and low death rates
Low birth rates and high death rates
Low birth rates and low death rates
58925.e: In pre-industrial societies, birth and death rates are both high. The population therefore grows only slowly.
58925.m: In the first stage, births and deaths are equally frequent.

58926.q: Why does the population grow particularly strongly in the early transition stage?
a: The death rate falls while the birth rate stays high
The birth rate rises while the death rate stays the same
Many people immigrate from neighbouring countries
Both rates fall at the same time and equally fast
58926.e: Better nutrition, hygiene and medicine lower the death rate first. The birth rate stays high for now, so the gap between the two rates opens up.
58926.m: The population grows strongly when the death rate falls before the birth rate.

58927.q: What can typically be observed in the middle (third) stage of the transition?
a: The birth rate begins to fall markedly
The death rate begins to fall for the first time
The death rate rises sharply again
The birth rate reaches its peak
58927.e: In the third stage the birth rate falls, for example because of urbanisation, education and family planning. Growth gradually slows down.
58927.m: In the third stage, the birth rate finally falls too.

58928.q: What is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate called?
58928.e: The natural growth rate is the birth rate minus the death rate. Immigration and emigration are not included.
58928.m: The natural growth rate is the birth rate minus the death rate.

58929.q: Which criticism is often made of the demographic transition model?
a: It is based mainly on the development of European countries
It does not take the death rate into account at all
It only applies to countries with mineral resources
It was only developed after the year 2000
58929.e: The model was derived from the history of Europe. Whether and how quickly today's developing countries go through the same stages is not certain.
58929.m: The demographic transition model is strongly shaped by Europe.

58930.q: A population grows by 2% a year. According to the rule of 70, after roughly how many years has it doubled?
58930.e: According to the rule of thumb, you divide 70 by the growth rate in percent. 70 ÷ 2 gives about 35 years.
58930.m: The doubling time is about 70 divided by the growth rate in percent.

58931.q: In the demographic transition model, which development contributes particularly to the fall in the birth rate?
a: Better education for women and urbanisation
58931.e: When women stay in school longer, more people live in cities and children are no longer needed as a pension, families have fewer children.
58931.m: Education and urbanisation lower the birth rate.

58932.q: What is described in some models as the fifth stage of the demographic transition?
a: The death rate is higher than the birth rate
The birth rate rises back to its starting level
The death rate falls to zero
58932.e: In the fifth stage more people die than are born. Without immigration, the population then shrinks, as in Japan.
58932.m: In the fifth stage, the population shrinks without immigration.

58933.q: What is shown in a population pyramid?
a: The population by age and sex
The population by income and occupation
The population by place of residence and religion
The population by education and language
58933.e: The population pyramid shows men and women on the left and right, arranged by age from bottom to top.
58933.m: A population pyramid shows the age structure by sex.

58934.q: What shape is the population pyramid of a country with a high birth rate and high mortality?
a: A true pyramid with a wide base
An urn with a narrow base
58934.e: Many births give a wide base, and high mortality makes the age groups narrow quickly towards the top. This creates the classic triangle shape.
58934.m: A wide base shows many children and a growing population.

58935.q: Which pyramid shape points to a shrinking population?
58935.e: In the urn shape, the youngest age groups are narrower than the middle ones. Fewer children are born than are needed to maintain the population.
58935.m: An urn shape shows an ageing and shrinking population.

58936.q: What does a bell-shaped population pyramid indicate?
a: A population that stays roughly the same
A population with many war dead
58936.e: In the bell shape, the younger age groups are about the same size. Births and deaths roughly balance each other out.
58936.m: The bell shape stands for a stagnating population.

58937.q: How can you recognise the baby boom generation in a population pyramid?
a: By a clear bulge at the age groups with many births
By a notch in the oldest age groups
By a wide base among newborns
By a narrow tip among the very old
58937.e: The large age groups born in the 1950s and 1960s form a noticeable bulge. Over the years it moves upwards into the older age groups.
58937.m: Age groups with many births form a bulge in the pyramid.

58938.q: Why is the pyramid usually wider on the women's side in the oldest age groups?
a: Women have a higher life expectancy
More girls than boys are born
Men emigrate more often in old age
Women are recorded in statistics more often
58938.e: On average, women live several years longer than men. That is why there are considerably more women in the oldest age groups.
58938.m: In old age, women outnumber men because they live longer.

58939.q: What can cause a clear notch in a population pyramid?
a: A drop in births during a war
A period with especially many births
58939.e: In times of war or crisis, fewer children are born and many men die. Such gaps remain visible for decades.
58939.m: Wars leave visible gaps in population pyramids.

58940.q: Why is a population pyramid usually slightly wider on the men's side in the youngest age groups?
a: Naturally, slightly more boys than girls are born
Boys are recorded in statistics more often
Infant mortality is much higher among girls
58940.e: Naturally, about 105 boys are born for every 100 girls. Because men later have a higher risk of dying, the ratio evens out with increasing age.
58940.m: At birth there are slightly more boys than girls.

58941.q: Which shape best describes Switzerland's population pyramid today?
a: Inverted funnel with a wide base
58941.e: Switzerland has a low birth rate and a high life expectancy. The middle age groups are wider than the youngest, which corresponds to an urn or onion shape.
58941.m: Because of its low birth rate, Switzerland has an urn to onion shape.

58942.q: What does the total fertility rate show?
a: The average number of children per woman
The number of births per 1000 inhabitants
The share of women of childbearing age
The number of births per hospital per year
58942.e: The total fertility rate shows how many children a woman would have over her lifetime if the current age-specific birth rates applied.
58942.m: The fertility rate measures the average number of children per woman.

58943.q: In industrialised countries, roughly how high must the fertility rate be for a population to maintain itself without immigration?
58943.e: Each couple must roughly replace itself, so have two children. The extra 0.1 makes up for deaths before adulthood and the slight surplus of boys at birth.
58943.m: In industrialised countries, the replacement level is about 2.1 children per woman.

58944.q: Roughly how old are women in Switzerland on average when they have their first child (as of 2023)?
58944.e: According to the FSO, mothers are on average just over 31 at their first child. In 1970 it was still about 25.
58944.m: Swiss women today usually have their first child after the age of 30.

58945.q: Which country had the lowest fertility rate in the world around 2023, below 0.8 children per woman?
58945.e: South Korea recorded a fertility rate of 0.72 children per woman in 2023. Reasons include high education and housing costs and long working hours.
58945.m: South Korea has the lowest birth rate in the world.

58946.q: Which continent has the highest fertility rates?
58946.e: Especially in countries south of the Sahara such as Niger, Chad or Somalia, women have on average five or more children.
58946.m: Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest birth rates in the world.

58947.q: Experience shows that what lowers the fertility rate most strongly?
a: Better education for girls and women
58947.e: Educated women marry later, are more often in paid work and are more likely to use family planning. This clearly lowers the number of children.
58947.m: Education for women strongly lowers the birth rate.

58948.q: How does the crude birth rate differ from the fertility rate?
a: It relates births to 1000 women over 50
It counts only births of twins
58948.e: The crude birth rate gives the number of live births per 1000 inhabitants per year. It therefore also depends on the age structure of the population.
58948.m: The crude birth rate relates births to the whole population.

58949.q: According to the UN, roughly what was the global fertility rate around 2024?
58949.e: According to the World Population Prospects 2024, the global fertility rate was about 2.2 children per woman. Around 1960 it was still about 5.
58949.m: Worldwide, a woman today has on average just over two children.

58950.q: A country has 60,000 births and 4 million inhabitants. What is the crude birth rate?
58950.e: 60,000 ÷ 4,000,000 gives 0.015. Multiplied by 1000, that is 15 births per 1000 inhabitants.
58950.m: The crude birth rate is calculated in births per 1000 inhabitants.

58951.q: What does life expectancy at birth show?
a: The average number of years a newborn will live
The age of the oldest person in a country
The average age of the whole population
The most common age at death in a year
58951.e: It shows how many years a newborn would live on average if today's death rates stayed the same.
58951.m: Life expectancy at birth is the average expected lifespan of a newborn.

58952.q: What does remaining life expectancy show?
a: The average years of life left from a certain age
The life expectancy of people abroad
Life expectancy in a hundred years
The age from which you receive a pension
58952.e: Remaining life expectancy shows, for example, how many more years a 65-year-old has to live on average. It is important for planning pensions.
58952.m: Remaining life expectancy counts the years of life left from a certain age.

58953.q: According to the UN, roughly what was global life expectancy at birth around 2023?
58953.e: According to the UN, global life expectancy around 2023 was about 73 years. In 1950 it was less than 50 years.
58953.m: People worldwide now live on average over 70 years.

58954.q: What was the main reason for low life expectancy in earlier centuries?
a: The cold climate of the Little Ice Age
58954.e: Many children died before their fifth birthday. This pulled the average down strongly, even though adults often lived to 60 or 70.
58954.m: Low life expectancy in the past was mainly due to high child mortality.

58955.q: In which world region is life expectancy lowest today?
58955.e: In countries such as Nigeria, Chad or Lesotho, life expectancy at birth is well below 60 years. Reasons are infectious diseases, poverty and weak health systems.
58955.m: Sub-Saharan Africa has the lowest life expectancy in the world.

58956.q: What is one reason why men's life expectancy is usually lower than women's?
a: Men more often have riskier health behaviour
Men live in the countryside more often
58956.e: On average men smoke and drink more and have more accidents. Biological factors also play a role.
58956.m: Lifestyle and biology explain men's lower life expectancy.

58957.q: Which event lowered life expectancy in many countries in 2020 and 2021?
58957.e: The Covid-19 pandemic led to excess deaths, especially among older people. In many countries life expectancy fell temporarily.
58957.m: The Covid-19 pandemic made life expectancy fall temporarily.

58958.q: What is usually the relationship between a country's wealth and its life expectancy?
a: The greater the wealth, the higher the life expectancy
The greater the wealth, the lower the life expectancy
There is no relationship at all
Only very poor countries have a high life expectancy
58958.e: Richer countries have better nutrition, hygiene and health care. The Preston curve shows this relationship, which flattens out at high incomes.
58958.m: Wealth and life expectancy are closely linked.

58959.q: Which country, together with Switzerland, is among the countries with the highest life expectancy?
58959.e: Japan, Switzerland, Monaco and Hong Kong have topped the rankings for years. In Japan women live on average over 87 years.
58959.m: Like Switzerland, Japan is among the world leaders in life expectancy.

58960.q: How does the Swiss Federal Statistical Office define the old-age dependency ratio?
a: People aged 65 and over per 100 people aged 20 to 64
People under 20 per 100 people aged 65 and over
People aged 80 and over per 100 people in total
People aged 65 and over per 100 children under 15
58960.e: The old-age dependency ratio compares pensioners with the population of working age. The FSO uses the age groups 65 and over and 20 to 64.
58960.m: The old-age dependency ratio compares older people with people of working age.

58961.q: How does the old-age dependency ratio change if the age limit used for the calculation is raised from 65 to 67?
58961.e: The 65 and 66-year-olds then count as part of the working-age group rather than the older group. The top number gets smaller and the bottom number bigger, so the ratio falls.
58961.m: A higher retirement age lowers the old-age dependency ratio.

58962.q: What does the youth dependency ratio measure?
a: Young people under 20 per 100 people aged 20 to 64
Young people under 20 per 100 people aged 65 and over
The share of young people in education
The number of school leavers per year
58962.e: The youth dependency ratio compares children and young people with the population of working age. Together with the old-age ratio, it gives the total dependency ratio.
58962.m: The youth dependency ratio compares the young with people of working age.

58963.q: Why is a rising old-age dependency ratio a challenge for the AHV (old-age insurance)?
a: Younger people automatically get lower wages
The number of newborns rises sharply
58963.e: The AHV works on a pay-as-you-go basis: the contributions of those in work pay the current pensions. If there are fewer workers per pensioner, financing becomes more difficult.
58963.m: A rising old-age dependency ratio puts pressure on pay-as-you-go pensions.

58964.q: What is the sum of the youth dependency ratio and the old-age dependency ratio called?
58964.e: The total dependency ratio shows how many young and old people there are for every 100 people of working age.
58964.m: The youth and old-age ratios together give the total dependency ratio.

58965.q: In what range was Switzerland's old-age dependency ratio around 2023?
58965.e: Around 2023, there were just over 30 people aged 65 and over for every 100 people aged 20 to 64 in Switzerland. The FSO expects a further marked increase.
58965.m: In Switzerland today there are just over 30 older people for every 100 people of working age.

58966.q: What does an old-age dependency ratio of 50 mean?
a: There is one older person for every two people of working age
Fifty percent of older people are in work
58966.e: An old-age dependency ratio of 50 means 50 people aged 65 and over per 100 people aged 20 to 64. That is one older person for every two people of working age.
58966.m: An old-age dependency ratio of 50 means two people of working age per older person.

58967.q: Which two developments are making the old-age dependency ratio rise in Europe?
a: Low birth rates and rising life expectancy
High birth rates and falling life expectancy
Strong immigration of young people and more births
Rising infant mortality and earlier retirement
58967.e: When fewer children are born and people live longer, the older group grows compared with the working-age group.
58967.m: Few births and long lives make the old-age dependency ratio rise.

58968.q: Which measure is most likely to lower the old-age dependency ratio in the short term?
a: Immigration of people of working age
58968.e: Immigrants are usually between 20 and 40 years old and so enlarge the working-age group. This lowers the ratio of older people to people of working age.
58968.m: Immigration of young workers lowers the old-age dependency ratio.

58969.q: During which period did China's one-child policy apply?
58969.e: The one-child policy was introduced in 1979/1980 to slow rapid population growth. At the end of 2015 it was abolished in favour of the two-child policy.
58969.m: China's one-child policy lasted about 35 years.

58970.q: What replaced China's one-child policy from 2016?
a: A ban on births in cities
58970.e: From 1 January 2016, all couples in China were allowed to have two children. The government wanted to slow the ageing of the population.
58970.m: From 2016, China allowed all couples two children.

58971.q: Since which year has China officially allowed three children per couple?
58971.e: In 2021 the Chinese government announced the three-child policy. Later the restrictions were largely lifted and births were supported with money.
58971.m: Since 2021, couples in China may have three children.

58972.q: Which consequence of the one-child policy can be seen in China's sex ratio?
a: A surplus of women only in cities
58972.e: Many families wanted their only child to be a son, because sons traditionally look after their parents in old age. Between 2000 and 2013, there were about 117 boys born for every 100 girls.
58972.m: The one-child policy led to a surplus of men in China.

58973.q: What is known in China as the “4-2-1 problem”?
a: An only child has to look after two parents and four grandparents
Four children share two rooms and one bed
Four provinces have two big cities and one capital
A family has four sons, two daughters and one grandchild
58973.e: Because of the one-child policy, an only child later faces two parents and four grandparents. The burden of caring for the elderly rests on few shoulders.
58973.m: In the 4-2-1 problem, one only child carries the burden of six older people.

58974.q: For which groups did the one-child policy in China usually not apply, or only in a relaxed form?
a: For ethnic minorities and many farming families
For all civil servants in Beijing
For couples with a university degree
58974.e: Many ethnic minorities were exempt. In the countryside families were often allowed a second child if the first was a girl.
58974.m: Minorities and farmers were often exempt from the one-child policy.

58975.q: According to official figures, since which year has China's population been shrinking?
58975.e: In 2022 China reported a fall in population for the first time in decades. More people died than were born.
58975.m: China's population has been shrinking since 2022.

58976.q: How was the one-child policy in China mainly enforced?
a: With fines and disadvantages at work
With tax gifts for large families
58976.e: Anyone who had a child without permission had to pay high fines and risked losing their job. There were also harsh state measures of force, which are regarded as serious human rights violations.
58976.m: The one-child policy was enforced with penalties and force.

58977.q: Which demographic problem does the one-child policy make worse in China today?
a: A sharp increase in the number of children
58977.e: Because of the few births since 1980, the share of older people is growing fast. China is ageing before it is as rich as Western industrialised countries.
58977.m: China is ageing especially fast because of the one-child policy.

58978.q: Roughly what share of India's population lives in cities (as of around 2023)?
58978.e: According to the World Bank, about 36 percent of Indians lived in cities around 2023. The majority still live in villages, but urbanisation is advancing quickly.
58978.m: Most people in India still live in the countryside.

58979.q: According to UN estimates, roughly how many inhabitants did India have in 2025?
58979.e: The UN estimates India's population in 2025 at about 1.46 billion. That is more than a sixth of the world's population.
58979.m: India has almost one and a half billion inhabitants.

58980.q: According to the 2019 to 2021 health survey, which Indian state had the highest fertility rate?
58980.e: Bihar in the north had about 3 children per woman. The southern states, by contrast, are clearly below 2.
58980.m: In India, the northern states have higher birth rates than the south.

58981.q: When did India's last full census take place (as of 2025)?
58981.e: The census planned for 2021 was postponed because of the Covid-19 pandemic. Current figures are therefore based on estimates.

58982.q: According to the 2019 to 2021 national health survey, what is India's fertility rate?
58982.e: According to the National Family Health Survey, the fertility rate was about 2.0. India is therefore just below replacement level, but keeps growing because of its young population.
58982.m: India's fertility rate has fallen to about two children per woman.

58983.q: Why does India's population keep growing despite a fertility rate close to replacement level?
a: Because of the population momentum of a young population
Because of massive immigration from Europe
Because of a sharply rising birth rate
58983.e: Many young people are reaching the age of starting families. Even with few children per woman, this produces many births, which is called population momentum.
58983.m: A young population keeps growing through population momentum.

58984.q: What is the economic opportunity that India has because of its high share of people of working age called?
58984.e: When the share of people of working age is high and the share of children and old people is low, the economy can grow especially strongly.
58984.m: Many people of working age offer a demographic dividend.

58985.q: Which Indian state is seen as a model with a low fertility rate and high literacy?
58985.e: Kerala in the south-west has high literacy, low infant mortality and a fertility rate below 2.
58985.m: Kerala shows how education lowers the birth rate.

58986.q: Which Indian urban region is among the largest urban areas in the world?
58986.e: The Delhi urban area has over 30 million inhabitants. Together with Tokyo and Shanghai, it is among the largest urban regions on Earth.
58986.m: Delhi is one of the largest urban regions in the world.

58987.q: What is the name of the informal settlement built on stilts in the lagoon of Lagos?
58987.e: Makoko is a slum whose houses stand on stilts in the water of the lagoon. It shows the consequences of rapid urban growth in Nigeria.
58987.m: Makoko in Lagos is a slum on stilts in a lagoon.

58988.q: Roughly how many languages are spoken in Nigeria?
58988.e: Nigeria is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world. The official language is English, and Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are also widely spoken.
58988.m: Over 500 languages are spoken in Nigeria.

58989.q: What share of Nigeria's population is younger than 15?
58989.e: In Nigeria, over 40 percent of people are children under 15. In Switzerland it is only about 15 percent.
58989.m: In Nigeria, more than two in five people are children.

58990.q: Roughly what was Nigeria's fertility rate around 2023?
58990.e: Women in Nigeria have on average over four children. The number is falling, but it is still far above replacement level.
58990.m: In Nigeria, women have on average more than four children.

58991.q: Roughly what is the median age of Nigeria's population?
58991.e: Half of all Nigerians are younger than about 18. In Switzerland the median age is over 40.
58991.m: Nigeria has a very young population.

58992.q: Which stage of the demographic transition is Nigeria in?
a: At the transition from the second to the third stage
58992.e: The death rate has fallen markedly, while the birth rate is only slowly beginning to fall. That is why the population is still growing strongly.
58992.m: Nigeria is growing strongly because the birth rate is falling only slowly.

58993.q: Which city replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991?
58993.e: Abuja was built as a planned city in the centre of the country, partly so as not to favour any of the large ethnic groups. Lagos remained the largest city and economic centre.
58993.m: Nigeria's capital is the planned city of Abuja.

58994.q: Where did Nigeria rank among the most populous countries in the world around 2024?
58994.e: After India, China, the USA, Indonesia and Pakistan, Nigeria comes 6th. The UN expects Nigeria to climb further.
58994.m: Nigeria is one of the six most populous countries in the world.

58995.q: What challenge does rapid population growth create for Nigeria?
a: It needs millions of new jobs and school places every year
There is a shortage of farm workers
There are too many care homes for older people
Pension funds are overloaded by many old people
58995.e: Every year millions of young people enter the job market. Schools, hospitals and housing must be expanded quickly.
58995.m: Rapid population growth requires many new school places and jobs.

58996.q: What was the share of people aged 65 and over in Japan in September 2024?
58996.e: According to Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs, about 36 million people were 65 or older in 2024, which is 29.3 percent. This is one of the highest shares in the world.
58996.m: In Japan, almost one person in three is at least 65.

58997.q: Around which year did Japan's population reach its peak of about 128 million?
58997.e: Japan's population peaked around 2008. Since then it has been shrinking, because many more people die than are born.
58997.m: Japan's population has been shrinking since around 2008.

58998.q: What is a society called in which over 21 percent of the population is 65 or older, as in Japan?
58998.e: According to a common classification, a society is ageing from 7 percent over 65, aged from 14 percent and super-aged from 21 percent.
58998.m: With over 21 percent over 65, Japan is a super-aged society.

58999.q: Roughly what was Japan's fertility rate in 2024?
58999.e: Japan's fertility rate fell to a record low of about 1.15 in 2024. This is far below replacement level.
58999.m: Japanese women have on average only slightly more than one child.

59000.q: What is a main reason why Japan's population hardly grows through immigration despite a labour shortage?
a: Its traditionally very restrictive immigration policy
The lack of airports and ports
A legal ban on Japanese people leaving the country
59000.e: For a long time Japan admitted only a few immigrants. The share of foreigners is much lower than in Switzerland, but has been rising in recent years.
59000.m: Japan has traditionally relied little on immigration.

59001.q: Which problem is particularly visible in rural regions of Japan?
a: Many empty houses and dying villages
A strong influx of young families to the countryside
A lack of cemeteries in small towns
59001.e: Young people move to cities such as Tokyo, and older people stay behind. In the 2023 survey, Japan counted about 9 million empty houses, called “akiya”.
59001.m: In the Japanese countryside, many houses stand empty.

59002.q: With which technology, among others, is Japan trying to make up for its shortage of care workers?
59002.e: Japan supports robots that help lift patients or keep older people company. This is meant to secure care despite fewer workers.
59002.m: Japan uses robots in care for the elderly.

59003.q: Roughly what is the median age of Japan's population?
59003.e: Half of the people in Japan are older than about 49. Japan therefore has one of the highest median ages in the world.
59003.m: Japan has one of the highest median ages in the world.

59004.q: What is an important economic consequence of ageing in Japan?
a: Rising costs for pensions and health
A sharply rising number of schoolchildren
59004.e: More and more pensioners receive benefits, while the number of people paying contributions falls. Social spending makes up a large part of the state budget.
59004.m: Ageing increases the costs of pensions and health in Japan.

59005.q: Why is Bangladesh particularly remarkable in population geography?
a: It is the most densely populated large country in the world
It is the least populated country in Asia
It has the oldest population in the world
It has the lowest population density in Asia
59005.e: Apart from city states and microstates such as Monaco or Singapore, no country has such a high population density as Bangladesh.
59005.m: Bangladesh is the most densely populated large country on Earth.

59006.q: Roughly what is the population density of Bangladesh?
59006.e: With about 170 million inhabitants on just under 150,000 km², that gives over 1100 inhabitants per km². Switzerland has about 220.
59006.m: In Bangladesh, over 1100 people live on one square kilometre.

59007.q: How do you calculate population density?
a: Number of inhabitants divided by area
Area divided by number of inhabitants
59007.e: Population density shows how many people live on average on one square kilometre. So you divide the number of inhabitants by the area.
59007.m: Population density is the number of inhabitants per square kilometre.

59008.q: Switzerland has about 9 million inhabitants on about 41,000 km². Roughly what is its population density?
59008.e: 9,000,000 ÷ 41,000 gives about 220 inhabitants per km². So Bangladesh is about five times more densely populated.
59008.m: Switzerland has about 220 inhabitants per square kilometre.

59009.q: Which natural condition makes the dense settlement of Bangladesh possible?
a: Fertile alluvial soils in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra
Large oil deposits in high mountains
A dry desert climate with oases
Extensive coniferous forests in the lowlands
59009.e: Most of the country lies in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra. The fertile soils and the monsoon allow several rice harvests a year.
59009.m: Fertile delta soils feed the many people in Bangladesh.

59010.q: Which hazard hits Bangladesh's dense population particularly hard?
59010.e: Large parts of the country lie only a few metres above sea level. Monsoon floods and cyclones threaten millions of people, and rising sea levels increase the risk.
59010.m: Bangladesh is severely threatened by floods and cyclones.

59011.q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Bangladesh?
59011.e: With over 20 million people in its urban area, Dhaka is one of the most densely populated cities in the world.
59011.m: Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh.

59012.q: How has Bangladesh's fertility rate developed since the 1970s?
a: It fell from over 6 to about 2 children per woman
It rose from 2 to over 6 children per woman
It stayed constant at about 4 children per woman
It fell from 3 to below 1 child per woman
59012.e: Thanks to family planning programmes, better education and health care, the fertility rate fell sharply. Bangladesh is regarded as a success story for this.
59012.m: Bangladesh has greatly lowered its birth rate in 50 years.

59013.q: Roughly how many inhabitants did Bangladesh have in the 2022 census?
59013.e: The 2022 census counted just under 170 million inhabitants. This puts Bangladesh among the ten most populous countries in the world.

a: Deaths in the first year of life per 1000 live births
Deaths before the 5th birthday per 100 children
59014.e: Infant mortality counts the children who die before their first birthday, per 1000 live births.
59014.m: Infant mortality counts deaths in the first year of life.

59015.q: Roughly what is infant mortality in Switzerland?
59015.e: In Switzerland, about 3 in 1000 babies die in their first year of life. Around 1900 it was still well over 100.
59015.m: In Switzerland, almost all babies survive their first year.

59016.q: Why is infant mortality seen as an important development indicator?
a: It reflects health care, hygiene and nutrition
It shows the number of hospitals per inhabitant
It measures the share of women in politics
It gives the gross domestic product per person
59016.e: Babies are very sensitive to bad water, malnutrition and a lack of medical help. That is why the figure says a lot about living conditions.
59016.m: Infant mortality shows how well a country cares for mothers and children.

59017.q: According to the UN, roughly what was global infant mortality around 2023?
59017.e: According to the UN group on child mortality, the global figure around 2023 was about 27. In 1990 it was more than twice as high.
59017.m: Infant mortality worldwide has more than halved since 1990.

59018.q: Which simple treatment saves many lives when babies have diarrhoea?
a: Oral rehydration solution made of water, salt and sugar
A cold shower after every meal
59018.e: The solution replaces lost fluid and salts. It is cheap and has saved millions of children from dying of dehydration.
59018.m: A solution of water, salt and sugar saves children with diarrhoea.

59019.q: What is meant by neonatal mortality?
a: Deaths in the first 28 days of life
Deaths in the first 12 months of life
59019.e: Neonatal mortality covers the first four weeks of life. The risk of dying is highest during this time.
59019.m: Neonatal mortality covers the first 28 days of life.

59020.q: What relationship often exists between infant mortality and the birth rate?
a: When infant mortality falls, the birth rate usually falls later too
When infant mortality falls, the birth rate rises permanently
The two figures are completely independent
High infant mortality lowers the birth rate
59020.e: When parents can be sure their children will survive, they usually want fewer children. This is a key element of the demographic transition.
59020.m: When more children survive, families later have fewer children.

59021.q: In a country, 50,000 children are born alive and 1500 die in their first year. What is the infant mortality rate?
59021.e: 1500 ÷ 50,000 gives 0.03. Multiplied by 1000, that is 30 deaths per 1000 live births.
59021.m: Infant mortality is calculated per 1000 live births.

59022.q: Which measure greatly reduced infant mortality worldwide in the 20th century?
a: The invention of the fridge for drinks
59022.e: Vaccinations, for example against measles, diphtheria and whooping cough, protect babies from deadly diseases. Together with clean water they greatly lowered mortality.
59022.m: Vaccinations protect babies from deadly diseases.

59023.q: Which region of the world has the highest infant mortality?
59023.e: In countries such as Sierra Leone, Niger or Somalia, many more babies die than the world average. The main reasons are infections, malnutrition and a lack of care at birth.
59023.m: Most infant deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa.

59024.q: Why do rich countries often recruit immigrants for insecure, low-paid jobs?
a: Hardly any local people can be found for these jobs
Immigrants are not allowed to pay taxes
Local people are not allowed to take these jobs
Immigrants do not need any training
59024.e: In industrialised countries, many local people avoid badly paid and insecure work. That is why there is a constant need for immigrants, for example in construction or agriculture.
59024.m: Demand in the destination country also drives migration.

59025.q: Which of the following is a typical pull factor of migration?
a: A labour shortage in the destination country
Drought in the country of origin
Persecution in the country of origin
High unemployment in the country of origin
59025.e: Pull factors are attractive conditions at the destination. If workers are lacking there, job vacancies attract immigrants.
59025.m: Pull factors attract people to a new place.

59026.q: What are causes such as war or poverty that drive people away from their country of origin called?
59026.e: Push factors drive people away from where they live. Pull factors such as good jobs attract them to a new place.
59026.m: Push factors drive people away, pull factors attract them.

59027.q: Which category did Everett S. Lee add to the factors in the area of origin and destination in his 1966 migration model?
59027.e: Lee stressed that between origin and destination there are obstacles such as distance, cost or border laws. Personal factors also play a role.
59027.m: Obstacles along the way influence whether people really migrate.

59028.q: What is migration that is made easier by relatives and friends who have already emigrated called?
59028.e: In chain migration, pioneers help those who follow with information, accommodation and work. In this way, communities from the same region of origin form at the destination.
59028.m: Networks of relatives make further emigration easier.

59029.q: What does the “migration hump” theory say about poor countries whose incomes are starting to rise?
59029.e: Rising incomes allow more people to afford the costs of emigrating. Only at higher levels of wealth does emigration fall again.
59029.m: A little more wealth can at first increase emigration.

59030.q: Which cause does neoclassical migration theory put at the centre?
59030.e: According to neoclassical theory, workers move from regions with low wages to regions with high wages. In the long run, migration evens out the wage differences.
59030.m: Neoclassical theory explains migration mainly by wage gaps.

59031.q: Why do families in poorer countries often send one member abroad to work?
a: To spread the family's income risk
To avoid paying taxes at home
Because the law there requires it
To sell the farm at home
59031.e: If the harvest fails at home or a job is lost, money from abroad keeps the household secure. Experts therefore often see migration as a joint family strategy.
59031.m: Families often send one member abroad to spread their risk.

59032.q: With which country did Switzerland sign an agreement on recruiting workers in 1948?
59032.e: The 1948 agreement regulated the immigration of Italian workers, who were needed in construction, industry and the hotel and restaurant trade. A similar agreement with Spain followed in 1961.
59032.m: After the Second World War, Italy was the most important country of origin for workers in Switzerland.

59033.q: What is the renewed increase in population in city centres after a period of people moving out to the surrounding area called?
59033.e: In reurbanisation, more people move back into city centres, for example because of short distances and cultural offerings. The city of Zurich has been growing again in this way since around 2000.
59033.m: Cities can grow again after a period of shrinking.

59034.q: What is the movement of people from rural areas to cities called?
59034.e: Rural exodus is often caused by a lack of jobs and services in the countryside. It is an important driver of urbanisation in many countries.
59034.m: Rural exodus makes cities grow and villages shrink.

59035.q: What is the shift of population from the core city to the surrounding urban area called?
59035.e: In suburbanisation, people move to the suburbs, for example because of cheaper housing or more green space. In Switzerland many municipalities in urban areas grew strongly in this way.
59035.m: In suburbanisation, the suburbs around cities grow.
